items.title: Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses to Steal API Keys and Administrator Credentials
items.summary: Security teams that run AI coding assistants may be exposing their most powerful credentials without knowing it. A new study shows that Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers can quietly change their own code after they are set up. If an attacker poisons just one package in that chain, they could steal API keys and administrator logins. MCP servers let AI assistants talk to other tools, such as firewalls, SIEM platforms and cloud consoles. To do this work, they usually hold the keys of the person who installed them. Attackers already know this. A malicious MCP server found in the wild has shown how easily one trusted tool can leak data. Researchers at Corelight noted the weakness while checking an administrator’s workstation. They did not find malware there. They found AI assistants running MCP servers with privileged access, and they asked where the code in those servers came from and how it got updated. The answer is in Corelight’s research , published on November 10, 2026. Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses The assistants launched their MCP servers with a one-step tool called uvx. It downloads a Python package and runs it from a single line of settings. The settings looked safe, because they named an exact release, a version number or a Git commit. The catch is that pinning the main package does not pin the packages underneath it. One community server had pinned its seven direct dependencies and even published a hash-locked file. But the launcher ignored that file and fetched the roughly 60 other packages fresh from the Python Package Index (PyPI) whenever it rebuilt its environment. Over five weeks, that one server was rebuilt 19 times and produced 15 different sets of dependencies. Of its 69 packages, 23 changed versions, including the cryptography library and the MCP software kit itself. Nobody had touched the configuration. Corelight saw the same drift on every server launched this way. Every one of those packages runs inside the same process as the server. That means any of them can read the API tokens, the user’s files and the network paths the server can reach. A bad update does not even need to be called. Some malicious packages run the moment Python starts. The risk is not limited to Python. Some vendors tell users to start a local proxy with npx and a “latest” tag. That fetches the newest version at every start. It also echoes the critical mcp-remote flaw rated 9.6 on the CVSS scale, where fast updates helped, but a hijacked release would spread just as fast. Corelight stressed that this is not a flaw in MCP itself. Each case came from a setup choice. Of the 35 MCP servers it reviewed, 23 had a recommended install that would pull dependencies fresh from a public registry. Why Package Hijacks Make This Worse Attackers go after whichever dependency is easiest to take over. That might be a maintainer account with a reused password, a phished token or a weak release pipeline. The bad version then looks like a normal update. Corelight pointed to past cases such as xz Utils, Ultralytics and Nx, where stolen tokens and keys were the prize. The Shai-Hulud npm worm is a recent example. It used stolen npm tokens to publish infected versions of every package a victim maintained. A June 2026 variant reached PyPI and went after cloud credentials, GitHub tokens and API keys for AI coding tools. In one wave, six bad releases were live for under 30 minutes. A server that rebuilds every couple of days, and starts on its own, has more chances to land in a window like that. This pattern matches wider reports of how attackers poison trusted software updates to reach developer and cloud secrets. A managed update has a build you control and a version number you can see. A launcher that rebuilds at start-up offers neither, and the server’s own version number never changes. Corelight showed how to spot the problem. DNS and TLS logs list the hosts that contact GitHub, PyPI and npm. In its lab, that left four hosts. Endpoint data then showed that only the administrator’s workstation installed PyPI packages, and it did so whenever an AI assistant started its servers. Those servers made more than 1,600 connections in a week to 11 management systems. The fix is to freeze the environment. Teams should pin to a commit, install from a hash-pinned lock file, launch the server directly and turn off start-up update checks. Corelight froze five servers and started them 457 times over two weeks, and their package lists never changed. Each server should also get its own account with the least access it needs, and a named owner should review updates on a schedule. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Use Domain github.com Code download hunting Domain codeload.github.com Code download hunting Domain raw.githubusercontent.com Code download hunting Domain objects.githubusercontent.com Code download hunting Domain pypi.org Package registry contact Domain files.pythonhosted.org Package file downloads Domain registry.npmjs.org npm registry contact Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. To do this work, they usually hold the keys of the person who installed them. Attackers already know this. A malicious MCP server found in the wild has shown how easily one trusted tool can leak data.

They found AI assistants running MCP servers with privileged access, and they asked where the code in those servers came from and how it got updated. The answer is in Corelight’s research, published on November 10, 2026.

items.title: CNCF Welcomes Adyen as Platinum End User Member to Advance Open Source Financial Infrastructure
items.summary: Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters across €1.39T in volume, Adyen brings production-scale fintech expertise to CNCF governance and open source projects Key Highlights Adyen joins the CNCF as a Platinum End User Member, gaining seats on the CNCF Governing Board and End User Technical Advisory Board. Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters with Cilium, Prometheus, and OpenTelemetry, Adyen brings production-scale operational expertise to the open source community. Adyen open sourced kubectl-rexec, a Kubernetes tool that supports auditable kubectl exec access for regulated cloud native environments. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 11, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced that Adyen , the global financial technology platform, has joined the foundation as a Platinum End User. The move comes as 87% of financial organizations report clear business value from open source, according to the FINOS 2025 State of Open Source in Financial Services Report , reinforcing Adyen’s commitment to advancing the open source technologies that help power secure, scalable financial infrastructure. Processing billions of transactions each year and €1.39 trillion in volume in 2025, Adyen is investing at the Platinum level to help advance the secure, reliable cloud native infrastructure that financial services require. Its participation brings the operating perspective of a global fintech platform to the open, vendor-neutral community shaping the technologies on which modern finance depends. “End users are the operational backbone of the cloud native ecosystem, and Adyen represents the pinnacle of high-scale, zero-downtime engineering,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters at a global scale gives Adyen unique technical insights. We are thrilled to welcome them as a Platinum End User and look forward to their leadership on our Governing and Technical Advisory Boards.” Adyen’s membership provides the cloud native community with a direct feedback loop from an environment where platform availability, performance, and security carry immediate financial weight. Beyond leveraging Kubernetes , Cilium , Prometheus , and OpenTelemetry across its global infrastructure, Adyen actively contributes solutions designed for regulated engineering teams. This includes open sourcing kubectl-rexec, a tool that adds strict auditability to Kubernetes container-access workflows while preserving native developer velocity. “Investing in the CNCF helps us to maintain full control of our technology,” said Pedro Oliveira, VP of Infrastructure. “When you operate at our scale, vendor lock-in isn’t an option, and having a seat at the table matters. Bringing our real-world experience to the community lets us help shape the tools we rely on every day, making them more reliable for us and for the broader ecosystem.” As a Platinum End User Member, Adyen will hold a seat on the CNCF Governing Board , which provides business, marketing, and budget oversight for the foundation. The company will also appoint a representative to the End User Technical Advisory Board , which brings end-user needs and perspectives to CNCF community discussions. To learn more about becoming a CNCF member, visit https://www.cncf.io/about/join/ . About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private, and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io . ### Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io

items.title: Meta Wins CNCF End User Case Study Contest for Accelerating AI Infrastructure Deployments From Hours to Minutes
items.summary: Using Argo CD and Kargo, Meta is building a GitOps platform to streamline application delivery across 100 Kubernetes clusters supporting AI research and inference Key Highlights Meta’s Cloud Foundation team won the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for its GitOps platform, built with Argo CD and Kargo to streamline Kubernetes application delivery. The new platform cuts routine application deployment times from more than four hours to minutes, streamlining the small team’s workflow through a simplified application definition while adding more advanced features such as automated deployment configuration, independent release promotion, and health verification. By separating application delivery from infrastructure provisioning, Meta is enabling independent application rollouts while retaining Terraform for infrastructure management. SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation ® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, announced Meta as the winner of the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for its adoption of cloud native technologies to accelerate application delivery across its AI infrastructure. Through a GitOps platform built on Argo CD and Kargo, Meta’s Cloud Foundation team is transforming how applications are deployed and managed across approximately 100 Kubernetes clusters supporting AI research and inference, reducing routine deployment times from more than four hours to minutes. “AI infrastructure is causing organizations to rethink how they manage applications across distributed environments,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “Meta’s approach demonstrates how open source technologies like Argo can help teams automate their application delivery, reduce operational complexity and scale infrastructure without adding unnecessary overhead. It’s a powerful example of how cloud native technologies are supporting the operational demands of AI at scale.” Meta’s Cloud Foundation team, composed of more than 15 engineers, supports approximately 100 Kubernetes clusters across multiple cloud providers and accelerator families. Previously, Terraform was used for both infrastructure provisioning and Kubernetes application deployment, tying even routine application updates to a lengthy infrastructure release process. The shared deployment model meant stalled rollouts could delay unrelated releases and lacked automated health checks to verify application status. To address these challenges, Meta began building a GitOps platform that separates application delivery from infrastructure provisioning. Terraform continues to manage infrastructure, while Argo CD reconciles application deployments against configurations stored in Git. Kargo orchestrates release promotion across environments, enabling independent rollouts, automated health checks and versioned release records that improve deployment traceability and recovery. “GitOps and Argo CD give our small team a great foundation, shaped by years of community experience in Kubernetes delivery,” said Phong Nguyen, Production Engineer, Meta. “We focus on connecting it to Meta’s systems and aim to share our own lessons along the way.” Meta also simplified application delivery by allowing developers to specify deployment requirements through a short application definition. The platform automatically generates Argo CD and Kargo configurations, enabling independent release promotion, automated health verification and deployment consistency without requiring application teams to manage complex configurations. Meta plans to expand adoption of its GitOps platform and transition to a centrally managed Argo CD service to reduce maintenance overhead across its Kubernetes fleet. The team is also exploring upstream contributions to improve container registry authentication and Argo CD performance in large clusters. To learn more about Meta’s implementation and results, read the full GitOps at Meta: How We Went From Terraform on Cron to GitOps for AI Infra case study. items.title: OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
items.summary: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster. A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart. How a sandbox is created and run On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail. Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue ( openshell/#1719 ) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator. Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018 ). OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back. OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team. OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 ( #522 and #523 ). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime. Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough , makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor , Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below). OpenShell Agent Substrate Origin NVIDIA Google CNCF Sandbox Voted in Sep 26, 2026 Voted in Sep 28, 2026 Main problem What may this agent do? How do we run thousands of mostly idle agents cheaply? Unit of work One sandbox per agent: a Sandbox, a workload Pod, and a supervisor Pod An actor: an identity plus a snapshot. When active, it runs in its own sandbox inside a shared worker Pod. Workers are designed to hold many actors (–max-actors defaults to 1,000), but the autoscaling demo notes that each worker holds one actor today Kubernetes building block Agent Sandbox. The gateway creates agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resources, and the Agent Sandbox controller reconciles them Its own WorkerPool CRD (ate.dev), which atecontroller turns into a Deployment of worker Pods. items.summary_html:
What OpenShell is

AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. 

OpenShell, started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project, is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML:

  • Filesystem: Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable.
  • Process: before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp.
  • Network: outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method.
  • Credentials: the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows.

For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox, the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster.

A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart.

How a sandbox is created and run

On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail.

Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue (openshell/#1719) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator.

Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018). 

OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path

The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission.

  1. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart.
  2. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs.
  3. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth.
  4. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state.
  5. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back.
  6. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails.
  7. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off.
  8. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed.
  9. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request.
  10. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back.

OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team.

OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate

Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 (#522 and #523). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime.

Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough, makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. 

Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor, Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below).

Three areas that will matter most to Kubernetes cluster admins::

  1. How detailed the policy is. OpenShell checks each request at a supervisor that serves one sandbox. It can let curl read GitHub issues and block curl from creating one. Substrate checks traffic at a shared egress gateway, per actor and per destination host. There is work underway to natively support OpenFGA policies and allow external policy.
  2. What Kubernetes can see. Each OpenShell sandbox is a set of Kubernetes objects, so RBAC, Kyverno, audit logs, and kubectl work on it. Substrate keeps actors, templates, and egress policies in its own API, backed by PostgreSQL, so the Kubernetes API server is not on the request path. Admission control sees Substrate’s worker pools, but not the agents or their egress policies.
  3. Isolation. Substrate requires a gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor sandbox for every actor; a plain container is not supported. That is what makes its snapshots possible. OpenShell runs a standard container with Landlock and seccomp, and you can require a stronger RuntimeClass for untrusted agents.

If your agents hold real credentials and reach production systems, and you need per-request control and policy on Kubernetes objects, look at OpenShell.

OpenShell’s RFC 0012, merged Sep 10, 2026, makes isolation a pluggable isolation backend, separate from the supervisor that enforces policy. The team has proposed building a Substrate backend (NVIDIA/OpenShell#3362). OpenShell would keep the policy, credential, and audit controls, and Substrate would add gVisor isolation and suspend and resume that keeps memory.

Two pieces are still open: a versioned transport for a backend that runs in a separate process, and a lifecycle operation that keeps memory. As of Oct 11 the issue is open. A contributor has +1’d it and asked whether the maintainers would accept it, but no maintainer has replied yet.

If it is accepted, you would get OpenShell’s per-request policy with Substrate’s density. Until then, the difference for admins is where policy runs. With OpenShell, Kyverno checks the sandboxes themselves. With Substrate, Kyverno checks the worker pools, and per-agent policy is set in Substrate’s own API.

What Kyverno adds

Kubernetes settings decide the sandbox Pod’s image, privileges, resources, credentials, and network rules. OpenShell checks some of these itself (step 6 above). RBAC and Kyverno, or other Kubernetes policy engines, help cover the rest.

Start with RBAC. If only the gateway’s ServiceAccount and the Agent Sandbox controller can create Sandbox resources, other users cannot go around the gateway. Cluster-admins still can. RBAC decides who can use which verb on which resource type. It does not look at what a request contains, and it cannot add defaults. So these questions remain:

  • Which images may agents run?

  • Can an agent receive a raw API key?

items.title: How to Export Logs with Amazon Athena
items.summary: Athena doesn’t store logs itself. It queries log files in S3, such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, load balancer and WAF logs, through tables you define. Normal query results are saved as CSV in your results bucket. To get JSON instead, wrap the query in UNLOAD … WITH (format = ‘JSON’): Athena writes newline-delimited JSON to an S3 prefix, and you download it. Plenty of AWS teams keep months of logs in S3 and query them with Athena rather than shipping everything to a SIEM. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. You need to run Athena queries (athena:StartQueryExecution and related), read the table definitions in Glue, read the source bucket, and write to an export bucket. Add kms:Decrypt if the logs are encrypted with KMS. Know the table and its partitions. A CloudTrail table is usually partitioned by region and date, either with partition projection or with partitions you’ve added. Athena bills by data scanned, so filter on partitions every time. A query without them can scan years of logs. A workgroup. Athena runs queries in a workgroup with a results location. UNLOAD writes to its own target, but the workgroup still needs to be set up. Export with UNLOAD UNLOAD ( SELECT * FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE region = 'eu-west-1' AND day = '2026/10/19' AND useridentity.arn LIKE '%suspicious-user%' ) TO 's3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/' WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE') Adapt the partition columns (region, day) to your table definition. The target prefix must be empty. From the command line: QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution –work-group primary \ –query-string “$(cat unload.sql)” \ –query ‘QueryExecutionId’ –output text) # wait until SUCCEEDED until [ “$(aws athena get-query-execution –query-execution-id “$QID” \ –query ‘QueryExecution.Status.State’ –output text)” = “SUCCEEDED” ]; do sleep 5; done aws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/ ./ct-1019/ –recursive zcat -f ./ct-1019/* > ct_1019.jsonl zcat -f handles both compressed and uncompressed output, in case compression was left at the default. If the query fails, the wait loop never ends. Check for FAILED too if you script this regularly. Why not get-query-results ? It works, but it returns rows as lists of strings, 1,000 per page, which you then have to stitch back into objects. UNLOAD gives you clean JSON in one step. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Query scans terabytes No partition filter Filter on the partition columns Error about the output location Target prefix isn’t empty Use a new prefix Access Denied Missing S3, Glue or KMS permission Check each one; KMS is the usual suspect Zero rows Partitions not loaded, or the wrong partition format Check partition projection or run MSCK REPAIR TABLE Output files won’t open as text GZIP compression Use zcat, or set compression = ‘NONE’ FAQ Is this the same as Amazon Security Lake? Security Lake uses Athena too, but with its own OCSF tables and Lake Formation permissions. Can I export raw CloudTrail files instead? Yes. items.summary_html:
Athena doesn’t store logs itself. It queries log files in S3, such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, load balancer and WAF logs, through tables you define. Normal query results are saved as CSV in your results bucket. To get JSON instead, wrap the query in UNLOAD … WITH (format = ‘JSON’): Athena writes newline-delimited JSON to an S3 prefix, and you download it.

Plenty of AWS teams keep months of logs in S3 and query them with Athena rather than shipping everything to a SIEM. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. You need to run Athena queries (athena:StartQueryExecution and related), read the table definitions in Glue, read the source bucket, and write to an export bucket. Add kms:Decrypt if the logs are encrypted with KMS.

Know the table and its partitions. A CloudTrail table is usually partitioned by region and date, either with partition projection or with partitions you’ve added. Athena bills by data scanned, so filter on partitions every time. A query without them can scan years of logs.

A workgroup. Athena runs queries in a workgroup with a results location. UNLOAD writes to its own target, but the workgroup still needs to be set up.

Export with UNLOAD 
UNLOAD (
  SELECT *
  FROM cloudtrail_logs
  WHERE region = 'eu-west-1'
    AND day = '2026/10/19'
    AND useridentity.arn LIKE '%suspicious-user%'
)
TO 's3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/'
WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE')

Adapt the partition columns (region, day) to your table definition. The target prefix must be empty.

From the command line:

QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution –work-group primary \
  –query-string “$(cat unload.sql)” \
  –query ‘QueryExecutionId’ –output text)

# wait until SUCCEEDED
until [ “$(aws athena get-query-execution –query-execution-id “$QID” \
  –query ‘QueryExecution.Status.State’ –output text)” = “SUCCEEDED” ]; do sleep 5; done

aws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/ ./ct-1019/ –recursive
zcat -f ./ct-1019/* > ct_1019.jsonl

zcat -f handles both compressed and uncompressed output, in case compression was left at the default. If the query fails, the wait loop never ends. Check for FAILED too if you script this regularly.

Why not get-query-results? It works, but it returns rows as lists of strings, 1,000 per page, which you then have to stitch back into objects. UNLOAD gives you clean JSON in one step.

  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review.

Security Lake uses Athena too, but with its own OCSF tables and Lake Formation permissions.

items.title: How to Export Snowflake Logs
items.summary: “Snowflake logs” means one of two things, and the export works the same for both. It can be security data your team stores in Snowflake tables. Or it can be Snowflake’s own audit trail, the SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE views such as LOGIN_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY. For small pulls, run the query in SnowSQL with JSON output. For anything bigger, unload with COPY INTO a stage using FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON), and download the files with GET. Snowflake’s own logs drew a lot of attention in 2024, when attackers used stolen credentials to log in to customer accounts that didn’t enforce MFA. Login and query history are now standard asks in an investigation. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Before you start Access to ACCOUNT_USAGE . By default, only ACCOUNTADMIN can read these views. Other roles need the IMPORTED PRIVILEGES grant on the SNOWFLAKE database, or one of its database roles. Latency and retention. ACCOUNT_USAGE views keep a year of history but lag behind by up to a couple of hours. For the last seven days with no lag, the INFORMATION_SCHEMA.LOGIN_HISTORY table function is an alternative. A warehouse. Queries and unloads need a running warehouse, and they consume credits. Filter by time. Option 1: SnowSQL with JSON output (small pulls) snowsql -q "SELECT * FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY WHERE EVENT_TIMESTAMP >= '2026-10-19' AND EVENT_TIMESTAMP < '2026-10-20'" \ -o output_format=json -o friendly=false -o timing=false > sf_logins_1019.json jq -c '.[]' sf_logins_1019.json > sf_logins_1019.jsonl Option 2: Unload to a stage (larger exports) COPY INTO @~/exports/login_history_1019/ FROM ( SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*) FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY WHERE EVENT_TIMESTAMP >= '2026-10-19' AND EVENT_TIMESTAMP < '2026-10-20' ) FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON COMPRESSION = NONE) OVERWRITE = TRUE; JSON unloads need a single column, which is why the query wraps each row in OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*). That function leaves out NULL fields. Then download from your user stage (@~): GET @~/exports/login_history_1019/ file:///tmp/sf_export/; and combine the files with cat /tmp/sf_export/* > sf_logins_1019.jsonl. The same pattern works for your own security tables. Swap in the table name and its timestamp column. What to look for in login history Look for failed logins (IS_SUCCESS = ‘NO’) in bursts, and password logins without a second factor (SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR empty). Note logins from client IPs and client types you don’t recognize. Then follow those sessions into QUERY_HISTORY to see what was read. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Object does not exist or not authorized on ACCOUNT_USAGE Role lacks access to the SNOWFLAKE database Ask for IMPORTED PRIVILEGES or a database role Today’s logins missing ACCOUNT_USAGE latency Use INFORMATION_SCHEMA.LOGIN_HISTORY for recent events COPY INTO error about columns JSON unload needs one column Wrap rows in OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*) Fields missing in the JSON OBJECT_CONSTRUCT drops NULL values Expected; absent means NULL GET fails Not run from SnowSQL or the Snowflake CLI GET runs from a client, not the web UI FAQ Can I do this in the web interface? Querying, yes. Downloads from the web interface aren’t JSON. The client route above gives you JSON lines. What about Snowflake event tables? Event tables hold logs and traces from your own functions and apps. Export them the same way as any table.

items.title: Criminal IP Launches New TI Feed App on Splunkbase for Automated Threat Detection
items.summary: Torrance, USA, November 11th, 2026, CyberNewswire Criminal IP , the AI-powered threat intelligence and attack surface management platform developed by AI SPERA, has launched the Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk. Available through Splunkbase , the app automatically correlates Criminal IP threat intelligence with firewall traffic logs collected in Splunk. The integration enables security teams to determine whether organizational assets communicated with malicious IP addresses and whether sessions were successfully established. It also expands Criminal IP’s existing Splunk ecosystem beyond individual IP lookups and fraud detection, helping SOC teams identify high-priority threats within their existing Splunk workflows. Connecting Threat Intelligence with Network Activity Security teams often receive large volumes of IP reputation alerts without enough context to determine whether a connection was attempted, blocked, unanswered, or successfully established. This can make it difficult to distinguish routine scanning from communications that require immediate investigation. The Criminal IP TI Feed app addresses this challenge by correlating inbound and outbound threat intelligence feeds with firewall traffic already indexed in Splunk. Network activity is classified according to observed session outcomes, including completed, unanswered, denied, neutral, and unknown connections. Severity is also determined using actual firewall activity. Detections without a completed session cannot exceed the watch tier, while critical detections indicate that a session with a malicious IP was successfully established. This helps analysts prioritize incidents with the greatest potential impact. Automated Correlation and Retrospective Detection The app downloads Criminal IP TI Feed data every three hours and runs correlation searches against firewall traffic every 10 minutes. Results are written to a dedicated summary index, allowing dashboards and alerts to operate without repeatedly searching large volumes of raw logs. A daily retrospective search compares the latest Criminal IP threat intelligence against the previous 30 days of firewall traffic. This helps identify historical communications with IP addresses that were not recognized as malicious when the activity originally occurred. Seven dashboards- Overview, Investigate, All Detections, IP Lookup, Trends, Alerts, and Health- provide visibility into affected assets, malicious IP addresses, traffic direction, session status, severity, detection history, and feed collection health. The app can also deliver consolidated Slack alerts grouped by malicious IP address and traffic direction. These alerts retain asset-level details, including session counts, timestamps, and transferred data, while throttling repeated notifications to reduce alert fatigue. Advancing Intelligence-Driven Security Operations By connecting external threat intelligence with actual network activity, the Criminal IP TI Feed app provides the context analysts need to identify which assets interacted with malicious infrastructure and which detections require immediate attention. Automating feed collection, log correlation, historical analysis, dashboards, and alerts reduces manual investigation and helps SOC teams respond to meaningful threats more efficiently. AI SPERA CEO Byungtak Kang stated, “Threat intelligence becomes significantly more actionable when connected to the network activity occurring inside an organization. The Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk helps security teams identify affected assets and prioritize incidents based on observed session behavior.” About Criminal IP Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed. Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake. Users can learn more and download the app from Splunkbase: Contact Michael Sena AI SPERA support@aispera.com

items.title: How to Export Databricks Logs
items.summary: As with Snowflake, “Databricks logs” can mean security data you keep in Delta tables, or Databricks’ own audit log in the system.access.audit system table. The simplest export for both is a notebook cell. Query with Spark SQL, write the result as JSON to a Unity Catalog volume, then download it with the Databricks CLI. Spark writes newline-delimited JSON, so the files are ready for upload. Databricks is increasingly used as a security data lake, and its audit log matters in its own right: who logged in, who created tokens, who changed permissions. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Access. Reading system.access.audit needs the system schema enabled for your metastore and a SELECT grant from an account or metastore admin. For your own tables, you need the usual Unity Catalog grants. A volume to write to. You need a Unity Catalog volume you can write to, for example /Volumes/security/exports/logtotal, and the Databricks CLI configured on your machine. Compute. A notebook needs a cluster or serverless compute. Filter by date so you don’t scan more than you need. Export from a notebook (spark.sql(""" SELECT * FROM system.access.audit WHERE event_date = '2026-10-19' AND action_name IN ('login', 'tokenLogin', 'generateDbToken') """) .write.mode("overwrite") .json("/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019")) Spark writes several part-*.json files plus marker files. Download and combine them: databricks fs cp -r dbfs:/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019 ./audit_20261019 cat ./audit_20261019/part-*.json > databricks_audit_20261019.jsonl For your own security tables, change the query: select from your table and filter on its timestamp column. Without a notebook , the SQL Statement Execution API can run the same query on a SQL warehouse and return JSON. Rows come back as arrays, with the column names in a separate manifest, so you need an extra step to turn them into objects. For anything sizable, the notebook route is simpler. What to look for in the audit log Look at logins and token logins from unusual IP addresses, new personal access tokens, changes to permissions and group membership, and workspace or cluster configuration changes outside normal hours. Downloads of notebooks or results in bulk are worth a look too. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix system.access.audit not found System schema not enabled Ask an account admin to enable it Permission denied on the system table No SELECT grant Ask a metastore admin for the grant Can’t write to the volume Missing WRITE VOLUME Use a volume you can write to Download includes _SUCCESS and other files Spark marker files Combine only part-*.json Huge, slow query No date filter Filter on event_date FAQ Is the audit log also delivered to cloud storage? Workspaces can deliver audit logs to your own storage as well. If that’s set up, you can copy those files directly. Does this work on workspaces without Unity Catalog? The system tables need Unity Catalog. Older workspaces rely on audit log delivery to storage, and you write to DBFS paths instead of volumes.

items.title: How to Export BigQuery Logs
items.summary: When security logs sit in BigQuery (from a Cloud Logging sink, a Google Workspace export or your own pipeline), export them with EXPORT DATA. It writes newline-delimited JSON to a Cloud Storage bucket, and you download that. For small results, bq query –format=json prints the rows directly. Either way, filter on the table’s time or partition column first, because BigQuery bills by data scanned. BigQuery is where many Google Cloud teams keep log history long after Cloud Logging’s default retention has passed. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. You need to run jobs (BigQuery Job User), read the dataset (BigQuery Data Viewer), and write to the export bucket. Know the tables. A Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery creates tables named after the logs, for example cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, often partitioned by timestamp. Workspace exports have their own schema. Check the cost first. Add –dry_run to a bq query to see how many bytes it would scan. If the number makes you wince, add a tighter time filter. Option 1: EXPORT DATA to Cloud Storage EXPORT DATA OPTIONS ( uri = 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*.json', format = 'JSON', overwrite = true ) AS SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity` WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP('2026-10-19') AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-20'); The URI needs a wildcard (*), because BigQuery may write several files. Download and combine them: gcloud storage cp 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*' ./audit-20261019/ cat ./audit-20261019/*.json > bq_audit_20261019.jsonl Option 2: bq query for small results bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --format=json --max_rows=10000 \ 'SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity` WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP("2026-10-19") AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("2026-10-20")' \ > bq_audit_small.json jq -c '.[]' bq_audit_small.json > bq_audit_small.jsonl –format=json prints a JSON array, which jq flattens to one row per line. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Query scans the whole table No filter on the partition or time column Filter on timestamp (or _PARTITIONTIME) EXPORT DATA fails on the URI No wildcard in the URI Use …/*.json Permission denied writing to the bucket Missing Storage object create rights Grant write access on the bucket bq output cut at 100 rows Default –max_rows Set –max_rows, or use EXPORT DATA Nested fields look odd Repeated and nested columns keep their structure Expected; it’s still valid JSON FAQ Is this the same as exporting from Cloud Logging? No. Cloud Logging has its own export. This guide is for logs that already live in BigQuery tables. Can I export a whole table without a query Yes: bq extract –destination_format NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON copies a table or a partition to Cloud Storage. For investigations, a filtered query is usually better.

cat ./audit-20261019/*.json > bq_audit_20261019.jsonl
Option 2: bq query for small results 
bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --format=json --max_rows=10000 \
  'SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity`
   WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP("2026-10-19") AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("2026-10-20")' \
  > bq_audit_small.json

jq -c '.[]' bq_audit_small.json > bq_audit_small.jsonl

–format=json prints a JSON array, which jq flattens to one row per line.

Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixQuery scans the whole tableNo filter on the partition or time columnFilter on timestamp (or _PARTITIONTIME)EXPORT DATA fails on the URINo wildcard in the URIUse …/*.jsonPermission denied writing to the bucketMissing Storage object create rightsGrant write access on the bucketbq output cut at 100 rowsDefault –max_rowsSet –max_rows, or use EXPORT DATANested fields look oddRepeated and nested columns keep their structureExpected; it’s still valid JSON
FAQ

Is this the same as exporting from Cloud Logging?

No. Cloud Logging has its own export. This guide is for logs that already live in BigQuery tables.

Can I export a whole table without a query

Yes: bq extract –destination_format NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON copies a table or a partition to Cloud Storage. For investigations, a filtered query is usually better.

items.title: CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Zero-Day Exploited to Steal NTLM Hashes
items.summary: Microsoft has patched CVE-2026-124194, an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication information when a specially crafted message file is opened. Microsoft classifies the issue as a spoofing vulnerability and rates it Moderate with a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5. The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to send a malicious message file and convince a victim to open it in an affected Outlook version. Outlook can then connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the external-content warning users would normally expect. During that connection, Windows may expose NTLMv2 authentication information that can potentially be abused to impersonate the victim. Contact Sales Microsoft confirmed that CVE-2026-124194 has already been exploited in attacks. However, the company has not disclosed the threat actors involved, the scale of the campaign, victim organizations, delivery infrastructure, or whether the stolen authentication material has been used for subsequent lateral movement or account compromise. The flaw was addressed as part of Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday release on November 10. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 on both 32-bit and x64 systems. CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, confirming evidence of active exploitation and establishing November 24, 2026 as the remediation deadline for applicable U.S. federal agencies. Security teams can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize threat intelligence, identify suspicious Outlook and NTLM activity, and accelerate detection engineering and threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-124194 by correlating Outlook activity with unexpected outbound SMB connections, NTLM authentication attempts to external systems, suspicious message-file execution, and subsequent credential or identity abuse. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-124194 analysis CVE-2026-124194 affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024. Microsoft assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N, reflecting remote accessibility, low attack complexity, no required attacker privileges, required user interaction, and high confidentiality impact. The vulnerability is classified under CWE-356, Product UI Does Not Warn User of Unsafe Actions. In practical terms, Outlook does not display the warning that should normally alert a user before the application accesses potentially dangerous external content. Exploitation begins with a specially crafted Outlook message file delivered to the target. The attacker does not need an account on the victim’s system or Microsoft 365 tenant, but the victim must open the malicious file. Microsoft specifically states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, meaning simply displaying the message in Outlook’s preview interface is not sufficient. Once the file is opened, Outlook can initiate a connection to a network location controlled by the attacker without presenting the usual external-content warning. This is significant because Windows environments can automatically attempt NTLM authentication when accessing remote resources. The resulting challenge-response exchange can expose the user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to the remote server. An NTLMv2 hash is not the user’s plaintext password. However, possession of authentication material can create several follow-on risks depending on the environment and the attacker’s capabilities. BleepingComputer notes that captured hashes may be subjected to offline password cracking, while Microsoft’s advisory warns that the leaked authentication information can potentially be used to authenticate as the victim. This makes the vulnerability particularly relevant to enterprise environments that still rely heavily on NTLM for file shares, legacy applications, remote resources, or internal authentication workflows. The CVSS score of 6.5 may initially appear relatively modest for a zero-day under active exploitation. The score reflects the fact that exploitation requires user interaction and primarily affects confidentiality rather than directly delivering code execution, integrity loss, or service disruption. Operational risk is nevertheless considerably higher because Microsoft has already observed exploitation and CISA has independently added the flaw to KEV. Security teams should therefore prioritize exploitation status over CVSS alone when determining remediation urgency. The CVE record identifies the following affected and fixed versions: Product Affected versions Fixed version Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise Vulnerable releases before the applicable November security update Current Office Security Release Microsoft Office LTSC 2021 Earlier than 16.0.14334.21048 16.0.14334.21048 Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 Earlier than 16.0.17932.21140 16.0.17932.21140 Both 32-bit and x64 installations are affected. Organizations using Microsoft 365 Apps should rely on Microsoft’s Office Security Releases information because build numbers differ across servicing channels. Microsoft published CVE-2026-124194 on November 10, 2026 and released the corresponding security updates through Patch Tuesday. The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before a fix became available. Microsoft credits a researcher using the moniker “nono” and security researcher Benoît Sevens with discovering or reporting the issue. SecurityWeek notes that Microsoft’s acknowledgment for Sevens references the use of Anthropic’s Claude AI model during the research. The available sources do not provide the exact date on which the vulnerability was privately discovered or initially reported to Microsoft. The CVE-2026-124194 PoC landscape remains less important than the confirmed exploitation status. Microsoft and the two supplied reports do not provide public exploit code or detailed reproduction instructions. Some third-party exploit aggregators have produced conflicting signals regarding newly published proof-of-concept material, so defenders should not rely on public PoC availability when assessing risk. Active exploitation has already been independently established through Microsoft and CISA. For CVE-2026-124194 detection, defenders should monitor endpoint and network activity together. One particularly valuable signal is OUTLOOK.EXE initiating SMB traffic toward an external or previously unseen destination shortly after a user opens an Outlook message file. Outbound TCP port 445 traffic deserves particular attention. Microsoft recommends blocking outbound SMB traffic to the internet as a general defense-in-depth control because it can prevent internal devices from sending SMB data directly to external hosts. Security teams can also review Microsoft’s NTLM Operational log under Applications and Services Logs/Microsoft/Windows/NTLM and audit outgoing NTLM authentication. Microsoft provides a policy specifically designed to audit or deny outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers. Useful behavioral hunting pivots include: Outlook initiating unexpected external SMB connections. NTLM authentication attempts toward internet destinations. Successful authentication to internal services shortly after suspicious Outlook activity. Message-file activity associated with unusual external network connections. Repeated authentication attempts involving the same compromised identity. New logons from systems or IP addresses inconsistent with the user’s normal activity. Defenders should avoid treating every outbound SMB or NTLM connection as proof of exploitation. Both technologies can still exist legitimately in enterprise environments. The strongest detections will correlate Outlook activity, destination reputation, user interaction, NTLM telemetry, and subsequent authentication behavior. Microsoft has not published campaign-specific CVE-2026-124194 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, attachment hashes, sender addresses, or filenames associated with the observed attacks. The identity of the attackers and their targeting remain undisclosed. This means organizations currently need to prioritize behavior-based hunting rather than static IOC matching. CVE-2026-124194 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install Microsoft’s November 2026 Office security updates immediately. Office LTSC 2021 installations should be updated to build 16.0.14334.21048 or later, while Office LTSC 2024 installations should run 16.0.17932.21140 or later. Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise users should verify that their servicing channel has received the corresponding current security release. Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should verify successful deployment rather than assuming automated Office updates have reached every device. Administrators should take the following actions: Inventory Microsoft Outlook installations across managed endpoints. Identify Microsoft 365 Apps, Office LTSC 2021, and Office LTSC 2024 systems that have not received the November security update. Deploy the corrected builds immediately and verify installation. Review endpoints that remained vulnerable while exploitation was active. Block unnecessary outbound SMB traffic to the internet. Audit outgoing NTLM authentication and reduce NTLM usage wherever operationally possible. Investigate unusual Outlook-to-network activity and unexpected authentication attempts. Educate users not to open unsolicited Outlook message files or attachments from untrusted sources. Blocking outbound SMB on TCP port 445 provides an important additional protection layer. Microsoft explicitly recommends preventing SMB traffic from leaving the corporate network unless there is a specific operational requirement for internet-hosted SMB services. Organizations should also consider restricting NTLM. Windows provides the Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers policy, which can first be configured in audit mode to identify dependencies before administrators begin blocking authentication. Abruptly disabling NTLM across an enterprise can break legacy applications and workflows. Organizations should therefore audit usage, identify legitimate dependencies, implement required exceptions, and progressively move authentication toward Kerberos or other stronger mechanisms. If suspicious exploitation is identified, merely installing the update is not sufficient to close the incident. Security teams should identify the affected identity and review authentication activity occurring after the suspected message file was opened. Look for unusual SMB connections, remote logons, lateral movement, access to file shares, VPN authentication, cloud sign-ins, and other services that accept the affected credentials. Where evidence suggests that authentication information was exposed or successfully abused, reset the relevant password and revoke active sessions according to the organization’s identity-response procedures. Additional privileged credentials accessible to the affected account should also be investigated. Endpoint, proxy, firewall, email, EDR, and identity logs should be preserved before remediation when compromise is suspected. Correlating these sources can help reconstruct the sequence from phishing delivery through NTLM disclosure and possible subsequent authentication. CISA added the vulnerability to KEV on November 10 and requires applicable federal agencies to remediate it by November 24, 2026. CISA lists known ransomware campaign use as unknown. FAQ What is CVE-2026-124194 and how does it work? CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability caused by Outlook failing to warn users before performing a potentially unsafe external-content action. An attacker can send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it. Outlook may then connect to an attacker-controlled network resource and expose the user’s NTLMv2 authentication information without displaying the expected warning. When was CVE-2026-124194 first discovered? Microsoft publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on November 10, 2026. The company credits researchers “nono” and Benoît Sevens, but the available public reports do not specify the precise date of the original private discovery. The vulnerability was not publicly known before Microsoft released the fix. What is the impact of CVE-2026-124194 on systems? Successful exploitation can disclose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to an attacker-controlled server. Attackers may potentially use the captured authentication information to impersonate the victim, attempt offline password recovery, or gain unauthorized access to services that accept the compromised credentials. The vulnerability does not itself provide direct remote code execution. Can CVE-2026-124194 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation, and CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, 2026. Systems running vulnerable Outlook versions remain at risk until the corresponding Office security update is installed. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-124194? Install Microsoft’s November 2026 Office security updates immediately, verify that affected Outlook installations are running fixed builds, block unnecessary outbound SMB traffic, and audit or restrict outgoing NTLM authentication. Users should also avoid opening unsolicited Outlook message files from unknown sources. Security teams should continue monitoring Microsoft’s guidance for updated details for CVE-2026-124194 as additional information about the exploitation campaign becomes available.

items.title: Meet the Magnet Forensics Training Team: Grant Hazell
items.summary: Our Training team continues to grow. In our latest “Meet the Forensic Trainer” blog, meet Grant Hazell, based on Perth, Australia! Want a chance to learn from Grant in the classroom? Learn more about what courses are offered through our Training & Certification portal . 1. Tell us about your life before becoming a Trainer. After a long career within military and policing environments, a move into training with Magnet Forensics was something I was hoping to achieve. I served for six years with the UK Armed Forces, before joining Suffolk Police in the UK in 2001. After seven years, I moved to the other side of the world and continued my policing career with Western Australia Police for 18 years, working in frontline response, education and digital forensics environments. 2. What made you want to be a Trainer? I have always enjoyed classroom environments and explaining things in a way which people can understand and grasp. I thrive on helping students progress and use the material they’ve learned in a practical and meaningful way. Being a qualified counsellor, I’m also very keen on looking after students’ emotional welfare regarding the anxiety and stress of training, especially in the face of difficult content and the sometimes difficult dynamic of training when personal life issues arise. 3. What type of training have you taken part in personally? What is your favorite part of the role? I have previously trained police personnel in legal, law and policy matters, ensuring they were fully aware of the powers and policies which underpin the role they perform. Since being employed with Magnet Forensics, I have primarily trained students in mobile device forensics, notably the GK200 course. 4. What excites you the most about a new class? The opportunity to travel to new places and meet new people, getting a feel for their needs both in an operational and educational perspective. 5. Do you ever learn anything from the students? Being new to the role, I know the only way to improve is to be the classroom – responding to questions, researching, learning the manuals and making mistakes. Mistakes can be daunting as an instructor, but they are crucial to self-development and ongoing professionalism. 6. Is there a particular moment that stands out the most to you in your career in the classroom? I recently taught my first solo GK200 class in Parramatta, NSW. The class was very diverse regarding experience and the questions were challenging. I found the entire experience very rewarding and although uncomfortable at times, crucial for my confidence. 7. What do students get out of training in person that they can’t get on their own? Students get direct access to not only my knowledge and experience, but that of the entire organization. Teaching in person also provides a valuable ‘personal touch’ and the ability to assess all students to ensure they’re grasping concepts and haven’t been left behind. 8. How prepared do you feel students are to use Magnet Forensics products after taking the training course? Every day, I plan on ensuring that the students can learn at least one thing they didn’t know prior to the lesson commencing. If they can understand the settings of Magnet Graykey, configure it correctly for their desired output, and prevent one device from rebooting and losing access to data, I consider that a success. 9. What is most unique about Magnet Forensics’ approach to training? The personal touch. Not only do Magnet Forensics trainers have a wealth of professional and technical knowledge, but they’re also able to relate to students and content, using real-world examples and lived experience. 10. Why do you think certification is important to examiners? Certification proves to the courts and other interested parties that an operator has the proficiency to use the forensic tool/methodology. It demonstrates that a student has not only attended a course but has personally invested in their own development by subjecting themselves to testing. 11. How do you manage to keep up with the latest trends in digital forensics? Being involved in conversations with other trainers has always been one of the best sources of information. Speaking to previous law enforcement colleagues about frontline trends, ensuring our own qualifications are current and displaying an enthusiasm to learn new material is crucial to maintaining currency. 12. What trends do you see coming down the pipeline in digital forensics? The trends will vary widely across the practice of digital forensics. The challenges of certain specialized domains such as vehicle systems and IoT analysis will continue to grow exponentially.

Our Training team continues to grow. In our latest “Meet the Forensic Trainer” blog, meet Grant Hazell, based on Perth, Australia!

Want a chance to learn from Grant in the classroom? Learn more about what courses are offered through our Training & Certification portal.

1. Tell us about your life before becoming a Trainer.

After a long career within military and policing environments, a move into training with Magnet Forensics was something I was hoping to achieve. I served for six years with the UK Armed Forces, before joining Suffolk Police in the UK in 2001. After seven years, I moved to the other side of the world and continued my policing career with Western Australia Police for 18 years, working in frontline response, education and digital forensics environments.

2. What made you want to be a Trainer?

I have always enjoyed classroom environments and explaining things in a way which people can understand and grasp. I thrive on helping students progress and use the material they’ve learned in a practical and meaningful way.

Being a qualified counsellor, I’m also very keen on looking after students’ emotional welfare regarding the anxiety and stress of training, especially in the face of difficult content and the sometimes difficult dynamic of training when personal life issues arise.

3. What type of training have you taken part in personally? What is your favorite part of the role?

I have previously trained police personnel in legal, law and policy matters, ensuring they were fully aware of the powers and policies which underpin the role they perform. Since being employed with Magnet Forensics, I have primarily trained students in mobile device forensics, notably the GK200 course.

4. What excites you the most about a new class?

The opportunity to travel to new places and meet new people, getting a feel for their needs both in an operational and educational perspective.

5. Do you ever learn anything from the students?

Being new to the role, I know the only way to improve is to be the classroom – responding to questions, researching, learning the manuals and making mistakes. Mistakes can be daunting as an instructor, but they are crucial to self-development and ongoing professionalism.

6. Is there a particular moment that stands out the most to you in your career in the classroom?

I recently taught my first solo GK200 class in Parramatta, NSW. The class was very diverse regarding experience and the questions were challenging. I found the entire experience very rewarding and although uncomfortable at times, crucial for my confidence.

7. What do students get out of training in person that they can’t get on their own?

Students get direct access to not only my knowledge and experience, but that of the entire organization. Teaching in person also provides a valuable ‘personal touch’ and the ability to assess all students to ensure they’re grasping concepts and haven’t been left behind.

If they can understand the settings of Magnet Graykey, configure it correctly for their desired output, and prevent one device from rebooting and losing access to data, I consider that a success.

The personal touch. Not only do Magnet Forensics trainers have a wealth of professional and technical knowledge, but they’re also able to relate to students and content, using real-world examples and lived experience.

10. Why do you think certification is important to examiners?

Certification proves to the courts and other interested parties that an operator has the proficiency to use the forensic tool/methodology. It demonstrates that a student has not only attended a course but has personally invested in their own development by subjecting themselves to testing.

11. How do you manage to keep up with the latest trends in digital forensics?

Being involved in conversations with other trainers has always been one of the best sources of information. Speaking to previous law enforcement colleagues about frontline trends, ensuring our own qualifications are current and displaying an enthusiasm to learn new material is crucial to maintaining currency.

12. What trends do you see coming down the pipeline in digital forensics?

The trends will vary widely across the practice of digital forensics. The challenges of certain specialized domains such as vehicle systems and IoT analysis will continue to grow exponentially.

I do this because I know that I may otherwise end up doing a lot of work before I realise that I have chosen an inadequate presentation method. Everything is dictated by the questions that are being asked of the multimedia evidence and the complexity of the case. This is a list of such considerations: Image or Video Authentication?
