If so, you may want to consider outputting tables in Amped Authenticate as well as the conventional report. Are you comparing questioned images with reference images in your analysis? Consider using the reference image tab and outputting comparative tables in Amped Authenticate as well as the conventional report. Are you highlighting visual inconsistencies? Consider using the Annotate Bookmark function in the Project Panel. Choose the report output mode. My personal preference is the HTML format. This does require you to include a folder with the included images and plots, but it allows hyperlinking much better than other formats (you can link to specific paragraphs or sections of the Amped Authenticate report). What Should a Forensic Authentication Report Include? I will go through these in more detail, but when you produce an analytical report for court, it is imperative that it follows criminal justice guidelines and a set structure. I would expect an admissible report to have, at the very least, the following sections: An introductory page with exhibit and case references. A witness statement and/or an expert witness declaration , listing the expert’s duties and responsibilities to the court. An index of contents. A summary of the case circumstances, instructions and final conclusions for quick reference. A list of the exhibits received and integrity verification (copying, hash verification etc.) An explanation of the methodologies used for the analysis : this should be explained in lay terms as much as possible (use practical examples, if necessary). A chronology of the analysis conducted with reference to the instructions received. Consider different chapters to address each set of instructions. The significance of your findings and how much weight do they lend to your final conclusions. Your final conclusions , based on the objective and factual analysis that you have conducted and your expert opinion on how it answers the questions raised by the evidence. Authenticate’s report is great at explaining the processes and tests conducted on the evidence but obviously cannot contain all of the above sections in full. You can either produce an analytical report and create hyperlinks to relevant sections in the Authenticate report, or you may even export it to an editable format (such as docx) and manually add any extra analytical content. The choice is yours. Analysis and Report Generation Let’s look at a case in which a number of images showing a theft were sent to the Police by the suspect himself. The image shows a person going through an inventory of items in a metal warehouse before he proceeds to remove a number of steel brackets. The suspect claims he is not the person depicted in the image and that’s his alibi. This information is important to us because, like in most cases, it helps direct our image analysis and investigation in the right direction. Open Authenticate and load your clip into the viewer. Remember that you can analyze multiple images in your AAP project, so you can create one report that contains the analysis of as many images as you like. I’ve loaded one of the images that I have been asked to assess for any traditional or AI manipulation. I have more images to analyze, but I will do one at a time. Try and follow the workflow chronology set out in the filters panel. There is a good reason why filters are in the order they are listed in the program interface. Visual Analysis: Identify and Annotate Suspicious Image Details I’ve added the Visual Inspection filter to my Project panel (step 1 in the image above), which I usually do as standard. This will ensure the original image is digitally printed in full in the report . In this instance, by zooming in to several areas of the image (hovering over the image and using the scroll wheel of the mouse), I noticed a visual anomaly with the right eye of the subject. It really looks more like a shark eye to me than a human eye, so I annotated the bookmark by clicking the “Annotate bookmark” button (step 2 in the image above). I used a Magnify object to enlarge this suspicious area of the image and also used a yellow arrow to highlight the eye in question (step 3 in the image above). When I generate the report later, t he bookmark will be annotated inside the document . If you wish to add some notes or commentary to your bookmarks, you can do so by double-clicking and adding a bookmark description, as shown above. In this instance, I also changed the bookmark status to “warning” as this bookmark clearly shows some suspicious findings. This is now red color coded due to its gravity and will also be highlighted in red in the report . File and Metadata Analysis: Compare Questioned and Reference Images In this instance, I was also given a reference image to compare with the questioned images. Authenticate has some very powerful comparison tools, which can highlight expected and unexpected differences (highlighted in black and red, respectively) with pretty much every filter output. Below, you can see I have conducted a file analysis showing metadata for both the questioned and reference image and their differences in every field. I then added this filter as a bookmark, marked its status yellow (“To check”) and added a description, explaining the reference image contains a thumbnail, camera make and model and time/date of creation, which the questioned image does not contain. Local Forensic Analysis: Investigate Image Manipulation Indicators Filters from the Local Analysis group can provide some factual evidence of manipulated regions in the image as they rely on strong forensic principles to output their results. In this instance, I applied an ELA (Error Level Analysis) filter. It shows the local differences between pixels of the original image and pixels of the same image resaved at a different JPEG quality to reveal local traces of JPEG quality differences. Our initial suspicion about the strange appearance of the eye is now backed up by strong evidence of this region having been added to the original image. Just like before, I have magnified the relevant area of the filter output and added a bookmark description to feature in my report . My approach with Local Analysis filters is to try and back up every finding with several filters within the same group. One filter alone can reveal inconsistencies that may be accounted for by technical reasons, rather than actual deliberate manipulation. It is important to remain unbiased and collect as much evidence as possible to strengthen the weight of your suspicions. In this instance, I found the RAW Conversion Watermark filter also points to the same area of the subject as inconsistent (shown above). But this filter is considerably different than the ELA . It highlights areas of the image not containing the invisible Adobe watermark that is introduced in original images when converted from RAW to JPEG. The fact that it highlights the same area as the ELA can really not be a coincidence. Image Deepfake Detection Analysis Amped Authenticate also features two AI-based deepfake detection filters. One analyzes the entire image for signs of content generated by diffusion models, while the other examines facial regions for signs of content generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Both filters provide a confidence score to help assess whether the analyzed content may be AI-generated. In this instance, the diffusion model deepfake filter outputted a confidence score of 0.51 (where 0 indicates no confidence at all, and 1.0 maximum confidence). However, this could be accounted for by the size of the manipulated region, which is too small compared to the rest of the image. As we are unbiased, it is important to state that this could also equally mean that the image is not a deepfake at all. The GAN Deepfake Detection filter was also applied and this reveals maximum confidence that the face of the subject has not been generated by a GAN. Mind that this does not necessarily mean that the face of the subject is real, simply that it has not been generated by this model. It could have been generated by a different model (for instance, a diffusion model), OR, quite simply, it could be a real face. Remember also that the Deepfake Detection filters are quick and easy to use, but should not be your only analysis tool, as they essentially output a machine opinion. In this case, the face of the person has been changed from the original image and generated by a diffusion model. It is likely that the manipulated area was too small to be detected by the filter. Other filters, though, using a more solid forensic approach, correctly detected the manipulated area. Below, you can see the original image before manipulation. How to Generate an Image Authentication Report Once you have added all the relevant bookmarks with descriptions and status flags, you can go to the File menu and select the “Project Properties” option. Here, you can add case and author information as well as customize the size of your report illustrations. You can then go to the Tools menu and select the “Generate Report” option. Select your preferred output format (HTML in this case) and customize other options such as adding hash values and file information, as well as the agency logo. Below, you can admire the key areas of our report, with all the factual data gathered and our expert opinions on the significance of the findings. Preparing a Video Authentication Case Let’s switch to video authentication for a little while. If we want to work on a video case, we need to use the Amped Authenticate Video Mode. The analysis and report generation are similar to the Image mode. However, we obviously need to perform some tests that are relevant to digital video, such as the analysis of compression and continuity. When preparing the report, we can include selected frames from different analyses to illustrate our findings. We can start by clicking on the Visual Inspection filter and bookmarking the frames we want to illustrate in the report. In the example below, I note a suspicious rectangular outline surrounding the area of the visual timestamp. I have bookmarked a couple of frames where this outline is more visible and adjusted the levels to increase the contrast in that area. These frames will all be printed in the report later . Video Metadata Analysis: Examine File History and Export Logs File and metadata analysis in the Video Mode is done via the Advanced File Info utility at the top of the filter list. For those of you familiar with Amped FIVE, this is the same utility available in that application. Unlike the Image Mode, the output of the utility does not go into the report. However, the utility offers a number of different ways to export your data into a disclosable document. Let’s return to the video we previously examined using the Visual Inspection filter. In the MediaInfo tab of Advanced File Info, we noticed that the file’s creation date is October 17, 2026. However, the timestamp displayed in the video indicates that the original recording was made on September 3, 2026, as shown above. This discrepancy suggests that the video may not be the original recording and could have been re-saved or exported at a later date. We documented this observation by clicking the Save to Log File button. We have also saved the contents of the Exif log, as this contains numerous indications that the video has been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro, as shown below. It is all starting to look very suspicious! Video Compression Analysis: Investigate Continuity and Editing Indicators We then performed a compression analysis to investigate the video further. Our initial suspicions were supported by additional evidence, which we can present in the report in the form of plots and compelling illustrations . We clicked on the Motion Vectors filter and then on the “Generate Plot and Table” button in the filter settings. The plot showed very high motion vector activity at around frame 300. This is consistent with a visual “jump cut” on the subject with the green shirt, even though the timestamp at the top right corner is contiguous. We then added frame 307 as a bookmark, added a description explaining the anomaly and marked the status as “warning”. We ticked both the image and the plot options to ensure both are digitally printed in the report . And finally, we clicked on the Macroblocks filter and found a few frames with suspicious intra-block activity (shown in purple in the image below) on the superior aspect of the frame. This suggests the frames in question were originally I-frames. When re-encoded, they left traces behind in the area where the alleged manipulation had occurred. In this instance, I only included the image and the table as no plot is applicable to my analysis . Video Deepfake Detection Analysis We finally clicked on the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter and ran the analysis to check if any portions of the video may have been generated synthetically. The analysis came back negative for all the frames of the video. In this instance, we added any frame as a bookmark and simply selected the plot and table for the report (as shown below). How to Generate a Video Authentication Report Once the bookmarks were reviewed and checked in the Project panel, I simply clicked on the Project Properties button to add case information and then navigated to the Tools menu and selected the option “Generate Report” (as shown above). As you can see, the report is quite comprehensive and contains all the relevant illustrations, plots and tables relevant to my analysis. I also included the Advanced File Info data, which I printed to PDF from the log files generated by Amped Authenticate. This allowed me to provide factual evidence that, although the video was not manipulated by any form of AI image generation, it had been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro. The actual crime (theft by employee) was cut from the video and the visual timestamp in the top right corner was laid as a rectangular crop to make it look as if the video was contiguous. Exporting Batch Analysis Results and Tabular Data in Amped Authenticate As mentioned earlier, there may be instances where your analysis involves multiple files (images or videos). You may have been asked to separate images that have been possibly manipulated from camera originals. Or, you may have been asked to conduct a batch comparison of images or a mass deepfake detection analysis. Authenticate’s report already supports multiple images or videos, but you may also want to produce tables containing data in a more granular format. Authenticate supports this workflow wonderfully. Let’s take a look at a case where I have been asked to perform camera ballistics on a folder full of images. Batch Image Analysis: Export PRNU Camera Identification Results The best thing to do when working with multiple clips is to simply load one of them in the evidence tab. Various filters offer options to analyze or compare all images in a folder and where this is the case, there will be a button at the top of the viewer. The filter will then output the data in a table that can be exported as an HTML or Excel file simply by right-clicking on it and selecting the appropriate option. The image below comes from a folder seized from a suspect’s computer. We also have his digital camera which we used to capture some reference images. Our goal is to determine whether any of the recovered images were taken with that specific camera, as some contain child sexual abuse material (CSAM). We applied the PRNU Identification filter from the Camera Identification group, loaded the camera reference pattern from the file generated with the reference images and immediately found the loaded image as positive with a high PCE (peak correlation energy) value. We then used the arrow buttons in the evidence tab to navigate to the other questioned images contained in the same folder. We found a second image positive, whilst all the others came back as negative. We added a bookmark for each of the two positive images so that the PRNU data will be shown in the report for both. But, we then clicked on the “Analyze all Images in the Evidence Folder” button and this outputted a table containing the results for all the images in the folder. I then right-clicked on the table and selected the “export as HTML” option. This wrote an HTML standalone file which I then linked to my master report. Conclusions We come to the end of this article and of the whole Court Presentation series. We really hope that this series gave you some food for thought when it comes to presenting forensic multimedia evidence in court. Remember, you may have found compelling evidence that images have been tampered with or manipulated with AI image generation. However, if you can’t present the factual evidence supporting your conclusions, even the strongest findings may fail to stand up to scrutiny in court. Amped products are designed to help you present and report your findings clearly and effectively, demonstrating to the trier of fact how your expert opinions are supported by scientific evidence. Throughout this series, we’ve explored practical workflows to help you achieve exactly that. If you would like to practice firsthand on the many presentation workflows we have in Amped Authenticate, Amped FIVE and Amped Replay, make sure you check out our training page where a number of courses relevant to court presentation are on offer at an affordable price. Until the next time, my friends, stay safe and take care. FAQ: Reporting Image and Video Authentication Findings for Court What should a forensic image or video authentication report include? Your report should clearly document the evidence examined, its integrity, the forensic methods applied, your findings, and the reasoning behind your conclusions. Depending on the applicable legal requirements, you may also need to include case references, an expert witness declaration, and supporting documentation. Amped Authenticate helps you generate technical reports with analysis results, annotated images, plots, and tables that you can incorporate into your final expert report. How can I document suspected image manipulation in Amped Authenticate? You can use Visual Inspection to identify suspicious details, then apply relevant forensic filters to investigate potential inconsistencies. Use bookmarks, annotations, and descriptive notes to highlight important findings. Where appropriate, compare questioned images with reference images and use multiple analysis methods to support your conclusions. How can I present evidence of possible video editing or manipulation? You can combine visual inspection with metadata, compression, and continuity analysis to identify potential editing indicators. Amped Authenticate allows you to document suspicious frames, highlight anomalies, and include relevant plots and tables in your report. You should explain what each finding indicates and consider whether alternative explanations are possible. Can deepfake detection results alone prove that an image or video has been manipulated? No. AI-based deepfake detection filters provide indications based on the models and methods they use, but their results are not conclusive proof of authenticity or manipulation. A negative result does not necessarily exclude AI-generated content. You should interpret detection scores alongside other forensic findings and clearly explain their limitations in your report. How can I include video metadata analysis results in my forensic report? In Amped Authenticate’s Video mode, you can examine file information and metadata using the Advanced File Info utility. Since these results are not automatically included in the generated report, you can export the relevant information to log files and incorporate it into your supporting documentation. Can I export forensic analysis results for multiple images or videos? Yes. Amped Authenticate supports the analysis of multiple files and the generation of reports containing their findings. For supported filters, you can also perform batch analysis and export tabular results in HTML or Excel format. This is particularly useful when comparing numerous images, conducting camera identification analysis, or reviewing results across larger evidence collections. https://blog.ampedsoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Evidence-prep-for-court-Ep.3-1.png

How to Generate an Image Authentication Report

Once you have added all the relevant bookmarks with descriptions and status flags, you can go to the File menu and select the “Project Properties” option. Here, you can add case and author information as well as customize the size of your report illustrations.

You can then go to the Tools menu and select the “Generate Report” option. Select your preferred output format (HTML in this case) and customize other options such as adding hash values and file information, as well as the agency logo.

Below, you can admire the key areas of our report, with all the factual data gathered and our expert opinions on the significance of the findings.

Preparing a Video Authentication Case

Let’s switch to video authentication for a little while. If we want to work on a video case, we need to use the Amped Authenticate Video Mode. The analysis and report generation are similar to the Image mode. However, we obviously need to perform some tests that are relevant to digital video, such as the analysis of compression and continuity.

When preparing the report, we can include selected frames from different analyses to illustrate our findings. We can start by clicking on the Visual Inspection filter and bookmarking the frames we want to illustrate in the report.

In the example below, I note a suspicious rectangular outline surrounding the area of the visual timestamp.  I have bookmarked a couple of frames where this outline is more visible and adjusted the levels to increase the contrast in that area. These frames will all be printed in the report later.

Video Metadata Analysis: Examine File History and Export Logs

File and metadata analysis in the Video Mode is done via the Advanced File Info utility at the top of the filter list. For those of you familiar with Amped FIVE, this is the same utility available in that application. Unlike the Image Mode, the output of the utility does not go into the report. However, the utility offers a number of different ways to export your data into a disclosable document.

Let’s return to the video we previously examined using the Visual Inspection filter. In the MediaInfo tab of Advanced File Info, we noticed that the file’s creation date is October 17, 2026. However, the timestamp displayed in the video indicates that the original recording was made on September 3, 2026, as shown above.

This discrepancy suggests that the video may not be the original recording and could have been re-saved or exported at a later date. We documented this observation by clicking the Save to Log File button.

We have also saved the contents of the Exif log, as this contains numerous indications that the video has been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro, as shown below. It is all starting to look very suspicious!

Video Compression Analysis: Investigate Continuity and Editing Indicators

We then performed a compression analysis to investigate the video further. Our initial suspicions were supported by additional evidence, which we can present in the report in the form of plots and compelling illustrations.

We clicked on the Motion Vectors filter and then on the “Generate Plot and Table” button in the filter settings. The plot showed very high motion vector activity at around frame 300. This is consistent with a visual “jump cut” on the subject with the green shirt, even though the timestamp at the top right corner is contiguous.

We then added frame 307 as a bookmark, added a description explaining the anomaly and marked the status as “warning”. We ticked both the image and the plot options to ensure both are digitally printed in the report.

And finally, we clicked on the Macroblocks filter and found a few frames with suspicious intra-block activity (shown in purple in the image below) on the superior aspect of the frame. This suggests the frames in question were originally I-frames. When re-encoded, they left traces behind in the area where the alleged manipulation had occurred. In this instance, I only included the image and the table as no plot is applicable to my analysis.

Video Deepfake Detection Analysis

We finally clicked on the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter and ran the analysis to check if any portions of the video may have been generated synthetically. The analysis came back negative for all the frames of the video. In this instance, we added any frame as a bookmark and simply selected the plot and table for the report (as shown below).

How to Generate a Video Authentication Report

Once the bookmarks were reviewed and checked in the Project panel, I simply clicked on the Project Properties button to add case information and then navigated to the Tools menu and selected the option “Generate Report” (as shown above). As you can see, the report is quite comprehensive and contains all the relevant illustrations, plots and tables relevant to my analysis.

I also included the Advanced File Info data, which I printed to PDF from the log files generated by Amped Authenticate. This allowed me to provide factual evidence that, although the video was not manipulated by any form of AI image generation, it had been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro. The actual crime (theft by employee) was cut from the video and the visual timestamp in the top right corner was laid as a rectangular crop to make it look as if the video was contiguous.

Exporting Batch Analysis Results and Tabular Data in Amped Authenticate

As mentioned earlier, there may be instances where your analysis involves multiple files (images or videos). You may have been asked to separate images that have been possibly manipulated from camera originals. Or, you may have been asked to conduct a batch comparison of images or a mass deepfake detection analysis.

Authenticate’s report already supports multiple images or videos, but you may also want to produce tables containing data in a more granular format. Authenticate supports this workflow wonderfully. Let’s take a look at a case where I have been asked to perform camera ballistics on a folder full of images.

Batch Image Analysis: Export PRNU Camera Identification Results

The best thing to do when working with multiple clips is to simply load one of them in the evidence tab. Various filters offer options to analyze or compare all images in a folder and where this is the case, there will be a button at the top of the viewer. The filter will then output the data in a table that can be exported as an HTML or Excel file simply by right-clicking on it and selecting the appropriate option.

The image below comes from a folder seized from a suspect’s computer. We also have his digital camera which we used to capture some reference images. Our goal is to determine whether any of the recovered images were taken with that specific camera, as some contain child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

We applied the PRNU Identification filter from the Camera Identification group, loaded the camera reference pattern from the file generated with the reference images and immediately found the loaded image as positive with a high PCE (peak correlation energy) value. We then used the arrow buttons in the evidence tab to navigate to the other questioned images contained in the same folder.

We found a second image positive, whilst all the others came back as negative. We added a bookmark for each of the two positive images so that the PRNU data will be shown in the report for both. But, we then clicked on the “Analyze all Images in the Evidence Folder” button and this outputted a table containing the results for all the images in the folder.

I then right-clicked on the table and selected the “export as HTML” option. This wrote an HTML standalone file which I then linked to my master report.

Conclusions

We come to the end of this article and of the whole Court Presentation series. We really hope that this series gave you some food for thought when it comes to presenting forensic multimedia evidence in court.

Remember, you may have found compelling evidence that images have been tampered with or manipulated with AI image generation. However, if you can’t present the factual evidence supporting your conclusions, even the strongest findings may fail to stand up to scrutiny in court.

Amped products are designed to help you present and report your findings clearly and effectively, demonstrating to the trier of fact how your expert opinions are supported by scientific evidence. Throughout this series, we’ve explored practical workflows to help you achieve exactly that.

If you would like to practice firsthand on the many presentation workflows we have in Amped Authenticate, Amped FIVE and Amped Replay, make sure you check out our training page where a number of courses relevant to court presentation are on offer at an affordable price.

Until the next time, my friends, stay safe and take care.

FAQ: Reporting Image and Video Authentication Findings for Court

What should a forensic image or video authentication report include?

Your report should clearly document the evidence examined, its integrity, the forensic methods applied, your findings, and the reasoning behind your conclusions. Depending on the applicable legal requirements, you may also need to include case references, an expert witness declaration, and supporting documentation. Amped Authenticate helps you generate technical reports with analysis results, annotated images, plots, and tables that you can incorporate into your final expert report.

How can I document suspected image manipulation in Amped Authenticate?

You can use Visual Inspection to identify suspicious details, then apply relevant forensic filters to investigate potential inconsistencies. Use bookmarks, annotations, and descriptive notes to highlight important findings. Where appropriate, compare questioned images with reference images and use multiple analysis methods to support your conclusions.

How can I present evidence of possible video editing or manipulation?

You can combine visual inspection with metadata, compression, and continuity analysis to identify potential editing indicators. Amped Authenticate allows you to document suspicious frames, highlight anomalies, and include relevant plots and tables in your report. You should explain what each finding indicates and consider whether alternative explanations are possible.

Can deepfake detection results alone prove that an image or video has been manipulated?

No. AI-based deepfake detection filters provide indications based on the models and methods they use, but their results are not conclusive proof of authenticity or manipulation. A negative result does not necessarily exclude AI-generated content. You should interpret detection scores alongside other forensic findings and clearly explain their limitations in your report.

How can I include video metadata analysis results in my forensic report?

In Amped Authenticate’s Video mode, you can examine file information and metadata using the Advanced File Info utility. Since these results are not automatically included in the generated report, you can export the relevant information to log files and incorporate it into your supporting documentation.

Can I export forensic analysis results for multiple images or videos?

Yes. Amped Authenticate supports the analysis of multiple files and the generation of reports containing their findings. For supported filters, you can also perform batch analysis and export tabular results in HTML or Excel format. This is particularly useful when comparing numerous images, conducting camera identification analysis, or reviewing results across larger evidence collections.

items.title: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
items.summary: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm called QuePaxa . QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and why it’s unique Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm. Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge. Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put . Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper. Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale . A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements . The challenges of consensus at a global scale While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable. Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers. Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues. Destructive interference and leaders Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits. Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal. Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance. When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony. To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast. The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place. When leader recovery is unstable When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system. Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again. Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader. Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure : a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other. Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime. When fault detection goes awry The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests. In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations. In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous. The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong. In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop . Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while. Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime. When fault detection is slow Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high. Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down. Why QuePaxa is the right fit We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa , published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al. The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers. In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders . Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see. Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely. The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round . However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal. One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional . The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip. However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same. This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers. However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make. If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures. How QuePaxa works under the hood To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works. QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases: Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately. Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders. Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it. Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders. Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders. The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem ), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority. In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection : any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal. Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3) : When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader. Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages. Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal. Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1 . If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received. Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round. This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round. Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence. Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide. No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving. How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted. The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt. QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster. What we’ll be showing next Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa. Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery . This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems. That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system. Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research .
