Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm called QuePaxa.

QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.

Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.

Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.

What we’re building and why it’s unique

Meerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.

Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.

Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.

Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.

The challenges of consensus at a global scale

While all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.

Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.

Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.

Destructive interference and leaders

Consider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.

Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.

Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.

When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.

To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.

The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.

When leader recovery is unstable

When a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.

Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.

Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.

Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.

Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.

When fault detection goes awry

The problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.

In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.

In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.

The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.

In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.

Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.

When fault detection is slow

Even when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.

Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.

Why QuePaxa is the right fit

We realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.

The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.

In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.

Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.

The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.

One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.

However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.

This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.

However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.

If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.

How QuePaxa works under the hood

To understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works.  

QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:

  • Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.
  • Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.
  • Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.
  • Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.

Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.

The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.

In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.

Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.

Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages.  

Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.

Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.

Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.

This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.

Moving to the next round:  After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.

Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.

No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.

How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possible

In our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.

The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.

QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.

What we’ll be showing next

Designing Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.

Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.

That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.

Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

items.title: Windows SignDrop 0-Day Exploit Lets Attackers Gain SYSTEM Privileges Through CLFS Protection
items.summary: A public exploit called SignDrop targets a Windows security feature meant to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS). It claims to turn a normal user account into a SYSTEM account, the highest level of control on Windows. The flaw has no CVE number and no patch as of November 11, 2026. Microsoft has also not confirmed the claims. Windows SignDrop zero-day exploit A researcher using the handle MSNightmare, also known as Nightmare Eclipse, posted the proof-of-concept on GitHub on November 10, 2026. The researcher has a history of public Windows exploit drops. Cyber Security News reported earlier this year that GitLab suspended the account after GitHub’s earlier ban. The researcher says the bug lives in clfs.sys, the kernel driver behind CLFS. It involves how the driver creates a “.cnpf” authentication file when a new log file is made through the exposed \CLFS device. The code uses object manager symbolic links and file timing tricks. It also claims a high-privilege Windows Defender process can be pushed into creating files in a protected place. CLFS Device Object Explorer (Image Source: Nightmare Eclipse) CLFS has long been a favorite target because it parses complex log files inside the kernel. A small mistake there becomes memory corruption, and that can lead to higher privileges. Cyber Security News has covered this pattern many times, including the CVE-2025-29824 zero-day that Storm-2460 used with PipeMagic malware to deploy ransomware. To cut this risk, Microsoft added a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) to CLFS log files. The code is built from the file data and a secret key unique to each system. If the code does not match, CLFS refuses to open the file, as Microsoft’s support page explains. This change reached Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 in updates released on or after October 28, 2025. New systems start in a learning mode, where CLFS adds authentication codes to old log files as they are opened. Microsoft says this period lasts 90 days from the first start with the updated driver. After that, the driver moves to enforcement mode on its next start. This is where the researcher’s claim comes from. MSNightmare says systems are exposed in either mode, so almost any machine older than 90 days would be vulnerable. The researcher also estimates that about 80 percent of Windows installations are at risk. Daily Security Review notes that this number is an estimate and not a measured count. SignDrop SYSTEM Privilege Escalation (Image Source: Nightmare Eclipse) Readers should keep a few limits in mind. SignDrop is a local privilege escalation bug, so an attacker must already run code on the machine as a normal user. It cannot break in from the internet by itself. The Rocket Boys review found no CVE, no Microsoft advisory, no independent test, and no sign of use in real attacks. It also did not run the code itself. The researcher reports testing on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 lab setups. The same review says the PoC does not work when CLFS authentication is turned off. That does not make disabling it a good idea. Do not switch off CLFS authentication to dodge this bug. Microsoft Learn says the setting is on by default, and turning it off lets the driver open and parse any log file, including crafted ones. That would bring back the older CLFS attacks the feature was built to stop. Instead, limit who can run code on important machines, and watch for odd file creation by Defender or other high-privilege processes. Also look for unexpected CLFS error codes such as ERROR_LOG_METADATA_CORRUPT. Admins can review the fsutil clfs command in Microsoft’s documentation before they change any settings. Treat SignDrop as a serious but unconfirmed threat for now. Microsoft will likely review it, and a fix would probably come through a Patch Tuesday update. Until then, the best step is to keep Windows updated and keep standard accounts tightly controlled. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .
items.summary_html:
A public exploit called SignDrop targets a Windows security feature meant to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS). It claims to turn a normal user account into a SYSTEM account, the highest level of control on Windows.

The flaw has no CVE number and no patch as of November 11, 2026. Microsoft has also not confirmed the claims.

Windows SignDrop zero-day exploit

A researcher using the handle MSNightmare, also known as Nightmare Eclipse, posted the proof-of-concept on GitHub on November 10, 2026.

The researcher has a history of public Windows exploit drops. Cyber Security News reported earlier this year that GitLab suspended the account after GitHub’s earlier ban.

The researcher says the bug lives in clfs.sys, the kernel driver behind CLFS. It involves how the driver creates a “.cnpf” authentication file when a new log file is made through the exposed \CLFS device.

The code uses object manager symbolic links and file timing tricks. It also claims a high-privilege Windows Defender process can be pushed into creating files in a protected place.

CLFS Device Object Explorer (Image Source: Nightmare Eclipse)

CLFS has long been a favorite target because it parses complex log files inside the kernel. A small mistake there becomes memory corruption, and that can lead to higher privileges.

Cyber Security News has covered this pattern many times, including the CVE-2025-29824 zero-day that Storm-2460 used with PipeMagic malware to deploy ransomware.

To cut this risk, Microsoft added a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) to CLFS log files. The code is built from the file data and a secret key unique to each system.

If the code does not match, CLFS refuses to open the file, as Microsoft’s support page explains. This change reached Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 in updates released on or after October 28, 2025.

New systems start in a learning mode, where CLFS adds authentication codes to old log files as they are opened. Microsoft says this period lasts 90 days from the first start with the updated driver. After that, the driver moves to enforcement mode on its next start.

This is where the researcher’s claim comes from. MSNightmare says systems are exposed in either mode, so almost any machine older than 90 days would be vulnerable.

The researcher also estimates that about 80 percent of Windows installations are at risk. Daily Security Review notes that this number is an estimate and not a measured count.

SignDrop SYSTEM Privilege Escalation (Image Source: Nightmare Eclipse)

Readers should keep a few limits in mind. SignDrop is a local privilege escalation bug, so an attacker must already run code on the machine as a normal user. It cannot break in from the internet by itself.

The Rocket Boys review found no CVE, no Microsoft advisory, no independent test, and no sign of use in real attacks. It also did not run the code itself.

The researcher reports testing on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 lab setups. The same review says the PoC does not work when CLFS authentication is turned off. That does not make disabling it a good idea.

Do not switch off CLFS authentication to dodge this bug. Microsoft Learn says the setting is on by default, and turning it off lets the driver open and parse any log file, including crafted ones. That would bring back the older CLFS attacks the feature was built to stop.

Instead, limit who can run code on important machines, and watch for odd file creation by Defender or other high-privilege processes.

Also look for unexpected CLFS error codes such as ERROR_LOG_METADATA_CORRUPT. Admins can review the fsutil clfs command in Microsoft’s documentation before they change any settings.

Treat SignDrop as a serious but unconfirmed threat for now. Microsoft will likely review it, and a fix would probably come through a Patch Tuesday update. Until then, the best step is to keep Windows updated and keep standard accounts tightly controlled.

items.title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More Certificate Authorities Following Major SSL Private Key Security Failure
items.summary: eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) after conducting a thorough review of the key issue that led to its October security failure. The new group did not have weak keys, but eMudhra could not prove the keys were handled the way its own rules require. The company has now pulled 16 intermediate certificates. The problem goes back to a key issue on 30 April 2025. According to reports, the keys were first created correctly inside a hardware security module, or HSM. eMudhra Certificate Authority Revocation A custom Python script then processed them to prepare a move to another device. A bug in that script shrank eight keys into tiny numbers such as 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. Mozilla’s public bug record explains why this was so bad. A P-384 private key should be a huge random number. Mozilla’s lead reporter found that all eight keys were smaller than 256, so anyone could rebuild them by simply guessing the first 256 keys. The same report says the script also made copies of eight other keys in an ordinary computer’s memory. Those keys stayed strong, but eMudhra said it could not show they were handled as its policy demands. So it revoked all 16 certificates tied to the affected keys. Mozilla’s bug thread lists the new batch, including intermediates named EM DV TLS CA – G2B and G2C, which sit under emSign Root TLS CA – G1. eMudhra added that this was the first time it moved keys between HSMs in different regions. It now creates keys without such transfers. According to the disclosure site by a researcher named Wayne, the weak keys were discovered on 17 October. He proved control by signing a short message with each key and sent it to the Mozilla, Chrome, Apple, and Microsoft root teams. Mozilla then rebuilt the keys on its own within hours, which proved the flaw was real and easy to use. Chrome and Firefox blocked the certificates that same day. Microsoft blocked them on 20 October, and Apple followed on 22 October, according to the disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson. eMudhra revoked the first eight on 18 October. Our earlier report on the eMudhra certificate authority compromise covers those first emergency steps. On 22 October, eMudhra said it would leave the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The company said no data was breached and that the affected intermediates had issued no website certificates.

eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) after conducting a thorough review of the key issue that led to its October security failure.

The new group did not have weak keys, but eMudhra could not prove the keys were handled the way its own rules require. The company has now pulled 16 intermediate certificates.

The problem goes back to a key issue on 30 April 2025. According to reports, the keys were first created correctly inside a hardware security module, or HSM.

eMudhra Certificate Authority Revocation

A custom Python script then processed them to prepare a move to another device. A bug in that script shrank eight keys into tiny numbers such as 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

Mozilla’s public bug record explains why this was so bad. A P-384 private key should be a huge random number. Mozilla’s lead reporter found that all eight keys were smaller than 256, so anyone could rebuild them by simply guessing the first 256 keys.

The same report says the script also made copies of eight other keys in an ordinary computer’s memory. Those keys stayed strong, but eMudhra said it could not show they were handled as its policy demands.

So it revoked all 16 certificates tied to the affected keys. Mozilla’s bug thread lists the new batch, including intermediates named EM DV TLS CA – G2B and G2C, which sit under emSign Root TLS CA – G1.

eMudhra added that this was the first time it moved keys between HSMs in different regions. It now creates keys without such transfers.

According to the disclosure site by a researcher named Wayne, the weak keys were discovered on 17 October. He proved control by signing a short message with each key and sent it to the Mozilla, Chrome, Apple, and Microsoft root teams.

Mozilla then rebuilt the keys on its own within hours, which proved the flaw was real and easy to use. Chrome and Firefox blocked the certificates that same day. Microsoft blocked them on 20 October, and Apple followed on 22 October, according to the disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson.

eMudhra revoked the first eight on 18 October. Our earlier report on the eMudhra certificate authority compromise covers those first emergency steps.

On 22 October, eMudhra said it would leave the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The company said no data was breached and that the affected intermediates had issued no website certificates.

Read more in our story on eMudhra exiting the SSL/TLS market. The company later cut its FY27 revenue outlook to about Rs 800 crore from Rs 825 crore and hired KPMG as an outside reviewer.

Mozilla and Chrome also moved to remove trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3. This protects tools that ignore revocation lists. eMudhra estimated about 30,000 certificates needed to move, and about 97 percent of them came through ACME, the automatic renewal system.

Apple fixed its developer tools issue on 10 November. Command-line tools such as curl and git on macOS now reject the bad certificates in macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3. Those updates also remove several eMudhra roots from the system file.

Microsoft has gone further. Its 10 November update says it will remove the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 starting 16 November.

Earlier, Microsoft had pushed an emergency Windows update, which we covered in Microsoft’s emergency update for eMudhra certificates. Oracle also shipped a Java fix for the same trust problem.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency would likely have caught a fake certificate. The disclosure site notes that many other tools do not.

These include curl, language runtimes, Electron apps such as Slack and Discord, and anything that ships its own certificate bundle. The site also says it is unknown whether anyone used the weak keys against these clients.

Update browsers, operating systems, and runtimes. Check any app, container, or build server that keeps its own trust list. On Macs, run the git and curl checks from the disclosure site after updating.

Admins should also watch for the 16 November Microsoft change if they still rely on eMudhra chains. The lesson is simple. Strong math doesn’t help if a small script bug weakens the keys, and a CA must test its keys before using them.

items.title: Remus malware claims Gmail access even after you change your password
items.summary: Changing your password should be part of recovering a compromised account. The developers of Remus Stealer are advertising a Gmail-reading feature they claim can survive that step and even session revocation. That is a serious claim. It is not, however, a demonstrated capability in the published investigation. Threat intelligence company Hudson Rock examined Remus’s promotional material and questioned both its developer and a self-described customer. Its conclusion is more cautious than the sales pitch: The material depicts a mailbox-reading interface, but it does not establish that Remus can retrieve new messages after an account has been comprehensively secured. Nor does it establish a Gmail zero-day vulnerability. What Remus is advertising According to Hudson Rock, Remus’s version 1.3.9 announcement promotes a feature that lets operators open a compromised Gmail mailbox directly from the service’s dashboard. The supplied screenshots show message lists, individual emails, and a “Mail” option attached to records of compromised devices. The announcement makes several additional claims: Operators can intercept email verification codes without collecting browser cookie files. Password changes and session revocation do not stop access. Mailbox access can be shared with other operators through links. Asked how it works, the developer described interaction with browser memory and said the malware executes and exits. The developer also claimed the service avoids Google’s anti-fraud checks, but withheld the technical details needed to assess that assertion. Remember, those are marketing statements from the seller of a criminal service, not independently verified findings. What the evidence shows Hudson Rock spoke with a person who had publicly endorsed the feature and described using it. That source said mailbox access continued after browser closure, a session reset, and a Google password change. But the correspondence does not document exactly which sessions were reset, the account settings involved, or the timing of the password change and subsequent access. The source’s independence was not established, and the statements were not accompanied by a controlled test. Hudson Rock explicitly states that its report includes neither reverse engineering of the new feature nor controlled post-recovery validation. Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know. SEE PLANS Can Gmail access survive a password change? Yes. Under some conditions, continued access after a password change is possible. Google documents that password changes ordinarily invalidate access tokens and refresh tokens used by applications with Gmail permissions. These tokens allow an application to access an account without asking for the password on every request. Token theft alone therefore does not establish that Remus can maintain access after a password change. What Gmail users should do The uncertainty around Remus’s claims is not a reason to abandon password changes. It is a reminder that recovering from an infostealer infection involves more than changing a password. If you suspect an infection or unauthorized Gmail access: Use a separate, trusted device to begin securing the account promptly. Disconnect the suspected infected device from the internet and remove the malware before signing in to accounts on it again. Change your Google password, review recent security events and signed-in devices, and remove unfamiliar access. Check applications with access to the account as well as device sessions. Inspect Gmail settings for unauthorized forwarding, filters, delegated mailbox access, and changes to remote mail access. Check your recovery email, recovery phone number, and verification methods too. Run trusted security software on the affected device. Google notes that resetting the computer and reinstalling its operating system is another option when dealing with harmful software. Review other important accounts that rely on the mailbox for sign-in or recovery, especially if you see unfamiliar verification or password-reset messages. A mailbox can be a stepping stone to other accounts because it receives recovery links and verification messages. But the Remus screenshots do not demonstrate a universal multifactor-authentication bypass, the ability to send mail, or complete control over every account associated with that address. Remus’s claimed persistence remains unverified. If you suspect an infection, secure your account and clean the affected device. items.title: N-able Releases Emergency N-central Hotfix After 33 Vulnerabilities Trigger Worldwide Shutdown
items.summary: N-able has released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 after the public disclosure of 33 alleged vulnerabilities forced a worldwide shutdown of its hosted remote monitoring and management platform. Released on November 10, the emergency update, build 2026.4.1.26, fixes seven published CVEs and adds security changes across the server, Agents, and Probes. The shutdown began on November 9, affecting hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able also advised customers running their own servers to take them offline. Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered the N-central shutdown and Able2Shell disclosure , which included public proof-of-concept code for attacks against the platform. N-able N-central vulnerabilities The research, published by Sean Bales through the Oracle-Security GitHub account, describes four exploit chains. Huntress reported that three could lead to remote code execution, while another could raise an attacker’s access to root. The research targeted N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected. One reported chain combines an XML external entity flaw with trusted session abuse to reset an account password and run commands as the N-able service account. Other paths involve malicious patch data, file upload weaknesses, and local privilege escalation. These paths matter because N-central manages customer devices, making server access valuable to attackers. N-able has observed scanning linked to the published exploit code, according to its incident update. Scanning alone does not establish a successful breach. Huntress’s updated report says hosted servers were upgraded and brought back online on November 10. Customers should not treat restored cloud access as proof that their own deployments are fully updated. N-able’s official release notes list fixes for XXE, OGNL injection, stored cross-site scripting, server-side request forgery, file repository path traversal leading to code execution, and two privilege escalation issues. The seven CVEs do not establish that all 33 researcher claims were individually confirmed or fully resolved. N-able has announced further security updates. The hotfix strengthens authentication, permission checks, file validation, server components, and web protections. It also removes legacy mobile device management and updates operating system and third-party components. Built-in remote control remains temporarily disabled, although Take Control continues working. Both hosted and on-premises customers must update Agents and Probes. N-able directs customers to upgrade Agents first, then Probes, because incompatible versions can interrupt communication and disable features such as offline patch caching. Older server releases require a supported intermediate upgrade. This follows a separate N-central authentication bypass incident reported in August. Administrators should follow the new release guidance rather than assume earlier hotfixes cover Able2Shell. Keep unpatched servers offline until their upgrade succeeds. items.title: Open code isn’t the problem: experts on the “god-tier” flaws exposed across UK government repositories
items.summary: A security researcher has uncovered more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, including credentials that could have given an attacker read-write access across an entire public body’s Microsoft 365 estate. The findings, first reported by WIRED , have reignited a long-running Whitehall debate: should government keep publishing its code at all? ControlPlane researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith examined 349 public-sector codebases belonging to 33 organisations and found serious weaknesses in roughly two-thirds of them. The problems were familiar ones – exposed credentials, missing access checks, overpowered service accounts and insecure defaults. What made the exercise notable was the toolkit: consumer versions of Anthropic’s Claude Opus and Sonnet models, run from a laptop. Nesbitt-Smith has stressed that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. All of the issues highlighted have since been disclosed to the organisations involved and addressed. For Olly Maxwell, principal security operations analyst at Huntress , the story is depressingly recognisable. “Having transitioned from Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office security to tracking EMEA threat actor tradecraft at Huntress, the recent WIRED report on public sector vulnerabilities strikes a very familiar chord,” he said. “Whenever stories like this break, the immediate political reflex across Whitehall is to lock down repositories and abandon transparent coding practices. That reaction fundamentally misunderstands both the root cause of the exposure and the reality of the modern threat landscape.” A “god-tier” key left in the history The most serious case involved the Planning Inspectorate, the agency that handles planning appeals and national infrastructure casework in England. An exported Azure Synapse notebook pushed to a public GitHub repository contained a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential. The integration it served only needed to retrieve a single HR file from SharePoint, but the permissions attached to it reached across every SharePoint site in the tenant and into private employee OneDrive accounts – including libraries holding evidence for statutory planning inquiries under legal hold. Maxwell is clear about where the blame lies. “Exposing tenant-wide Microsoft Entra ID credentials in a public GitHub repository is not a byproduct of open source philosophy. It is a severe breakdown in basic supply chain governance and DevSecOps hygiene.” Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solution management at Black Duck , points to the permissions model as the factor that turned a leaked secret into a potential catastrophe. “This is mostly the result of a failure to implement least privilege and implicit trust controls. Excessive permissions are what made the Planning Inspectorate leak dangerous: ControlPlane found that a pipeline needing one file had write access to every SharePoint site and to OneDrive.” He added that the pattern is far from isolated: “Broad application permissions have amplified other incidents this year: in October, Huntress confirmed unauthorised sign-ins in at least 162 Microsoft 365 tenants through one compromised backup-application credential. An application credential signs in with no user and no second factor. Microsoft Entra ID treats whoever holds the secret as the application.” Deleted from the branch, not from the identity provider Crucially, the credential had been removed from the repository’s branch – but not revoked. An orphaned commit remained retrievable through GitHub’s raw-content infrastructure for around 18 months, and the secret still worked. The Planning Inspectorate said its monitoring detected the researcher’s activity, that it treated the report as a cyber incident and revoked the credential roughly 20 minutes after receiving it on 26 August, and that it found no evidence of a data breach. “A force push removes the file from the branch, not the secret from Microsoft Entra ID,” said Hogue-Spears. “When a researcher used the secret 18 months after the force push, the Planning Inspectorate’s monitoring flagged the activity, and the agency revoked the secret about 20 minutes after the report.” Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck , argues that the episode exposes a design assumption rather than a coding slip. “This is a classic example of security being built, at least in part, on obscurity. The problem isn’t that the code was public, and it’s easy to point at AI as the culprit. Realistically, this isn’t an AI problem or an open-source problem. It’s a security architecture problem. The organisation implicitly relied on the assumption that these weaknesses, credentials, and excessive permissions wouldn’t be discovered. AI simply made discovering them faster and cheaper.” AI changes the economics, not the mistakes The use of off-the-shelf AI has inevitably drawn headlines, and it lands in a year in which the UK government has itself leaned on frontier models to hunt for flaws. In June, the Government Cyber Coordination Centre published results from internal hackathons that surfaced 407 findings across public repositories in nine departments, and in October an AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP vulnerabilities forced dozens of public sector sites offline. Maxwell believes the Nesbitt-Smith findings should change how defenders model the threat. “The fact that a researcher identified over 100 serious flaws across dozens of public bodies using consumer grade AI on a laptop should serve as a wakeup call regarding threat asymmetry. AI did not introduce these vulnerabilities, but it has completely democratised the cost of discovering them,” he said. “Public code repositories are subjected to continuous, automated scraping by hostile state nexus groups and initial access brokers. If an independent researcher can surface these gaps trivially, the operational assumption must be that adversaries have already mirrored the repositories and harvested the exposed key material.” Hogue-Spears points to evidence that this is already happening at scale. “Attackers search public code for application secrets. In a separate campaign Microsoft reported on November 5, threat actors used an agentic AI framework to search GitHub for secrets, often by organisation name, and then signed in as the exposed applications.” And the danger, Maxwell warns, is not necessarily immediate. “Crucially, highly capable threat actors do not always exploit this access immediately. They bank valid administrative keys and quietly establish strategic persistence within environments like SharePoint or legal hold libraries, holding that access until it becomes geopolitically or financially advantageous to strike.” Lewis echoes the point that AI is an accelerant rather than a cause. “‘Security by obscurity’ as a design choice is dangerous in the age of AI, but AI isn’t the root cause. An important takeaway for businesses is that ‘hard to find’ can no longer be treated as a security control. Organizations should assume that anything exposed to the internet, including source code, APIs, configurations and credentials, will eventually be analysed by AI. The barrier to doing that kind of analysis is rapidly disappearing.” Rushed delivery and deferred security Government has defaulted to publishing the code it produces with public money for around a decade, on the grounds that it improves transparency and makes reuse cheaper. But funding pressure has left many departments struggling to maintain their technology estates – and much of the build work is outsourced. “The rapid push to modernise government digital services relies heavily on third party systems integrators and outsourced development,” said Maxwell. “When aggressive delivery milestones collide with public sector funding squeezes, foundational security controls like automated secret scanning and identity posture management are routinely treated as deferred technical debt. The procurement lag for security tooling frequently eclipses the operational lifecycle of the product itself.” “These exposures happen because code is rushed into production environments before proper governance and risk compliance principles are applied. Securing modern CI/CD pipelines requires specialized knowledge to enforce pre commit security gates and token lifecycle management. Without those guardrails natively embedded into the developer workflow, credential sprawl is inevitable.” Lewis agrees that the answer lies in the basics. “Another important note is that this highlights the need for getting the fundamentals right. Secrets shouldn’t live in source code. Credentials should be short-lived and rotated. Identity should follow least privilege. A compromised credential shouldn’t provide broad access across the enterprise. And organisations need automated controls in the development pipeline that can identify these problems before code is published or deployed.” For Hogue-Spears, that means removing long-lived secrets from pipelines altogether. “Security leaders must move pipelines to managed identities or workload identity federation, which leave no secret to commit. A managed identity keeps whatever permissions an administrator grants it, so replace tenant-wide Microsoft Graph permissions with selected permissions scoped to the site or file the application needs. Treat any secret that reaches a public repository as compromised and revoke it in the identity provider before anyone cleans the Git history.” Beyond leaked credentials Not every finding involved a secret. At the Department for Education, the Get Help Buying for Schools service allowed anyone holding a valid request identifier to change request details – including the contact email – and submit the request without signing in; it was fixed on 10 July. In the department’s teacher application service, an account-linking code could overwrite an existing login association. Elsewhere, a long-lived administrator token was found embedded in public JavaScript on a Scottish Government open data portal, which has since been decommissioned. Hogue-Spears highlighted a further DfE case as a lesson in authorisation testing. “In the Department for Education’s training-provider register, delete actions ran with no authorisation check, so a low-privileged staff account was able to soft-delete registered providers and other staff accounts. The same service’s user-editing policy did run, and it examined the record’s state, not the caller’s role, so a standard staff account was able to deactivate an administrator’s account. The department fixed both flaws in July. If your tests never sign in as an ordinary user and attempt an administrator’s action, a missing check and a wrong check both ship.” Why closing the code won’t close the gap The findings arrive as some in government question whether public bodies should keep repositories open in an era of AI-accelerated discovery. Nesbitt-Smith himself has warned that pulling code private without fixing the flaws could make risks harder to spot. The experts are unanimous on this point. “Making a repository private hides the code, and a secret that leaked while the repository was public stays valid until it expires or someone revokes it,” said Hogue-Spears. “Leaders have to name an owner for every public repository. Since May, the UK government guidance has set a minimum before code goes public: a named owner and controls that stop developers from committing secrets.” Maxwell is blunter. “Consequently, advising departments to pull their codebases private without remediating the underlying architectural flaws is incredibly dangerous. Security by obscurity has never stopped an advanced persistent threat. Closing the repositories simply blinds the independent research community that provides vital early warnings, while doing absolutely nothing to evict threat actors who already hold the compromised credentials.” Lewis argues the real shift is in mindset. “Although there’s a knee jerk to blame AI for discovering weaknesses like this; in reality, a motivated attacker could have found these. AI doesn’t make design decision more dangerous; it simply changes the economics. In short, AI allows someone to search for existing mistakes, just faster, cheaper and at a scale that wasn’t practical in the past. And perhaps the most important lessons learned from this is that businesses need to operate under the assumption that if a weakness is discoverable, someone will eventually find it.” Maxwell leaves the final word with a call for discipline rather than retreat. “We operate in a climate where the UK faces continuous, hostile cyber activity. There is a vast difference between falling victim to a highly sophisticated zero day exploit and simply handing adversaries your production logins. The government does not need to retreat into the shadows. It needs to mandate strict, automated security gates across the entire software supply chain and treat identity security with the rigorous operational discipline it demands.”

Hogue-Spears points to evidence that this is already happening at scale. “Attackers search public code for application secrets. In a separate campaign Microsoft reported on November 5, threat actors used an agentic AI framework to search GitHub for secrets, often by organisation name, and then signed in as the exposed applications.”

And the danger, Maxwell warns, is not necessarily immediate. “Crucially, highly capable threat actors do not always exploit this access immediately. They bank valid administrative keys and quietly establish strategic persistence within environments like SharePoint or legal hold libraries, holding that access until it becomes geopolitically or financially advantageous to strike.”

Lewis echoes the point that AI is an accelerant rather than a cause. “‘Security by obscurity’ as a design choice is dangerous in the age of AI, but AI isn’t the root cause. An important takeaway for businesses is that ‘hard to find’ can no longer be treated as a security control. Organizations should assume that anything exposed to the internet, including source code, APIs, configurations and credentials, will eventually be analysed by AI. The barrier to doing that kind of analysis is rapidly disappearing.”

Rushed delivery and deferred security

Government has defaulted to publishing the code it produces with public money for around a decade, on the grounds that it improves transparency and makes reuse cheaper. But funding pressure has left many departments struggling to maintain their technology estates – and much of the build work is outsourced.

“The rapid push to modernise government digital services relies heavily on third party systems integrators and outsourced development,” said Maxwell. “When aggressive delivery milestones collide with public sector funding squeezes, foundational security controls like automated secret scanning and identity posture management are routinely treated as deferred technical debt. The procurement lag for security tooling frequently eclipses the operational lifecycle of the product itself.”

“These exposures happen because code is rushed into production environments before proper governance and risk compliance principles are applied. Securing modern CI/CD pipelines requires specialized knowledge to enforce pre commit security gates and token lifecycle management. Without those guardrails natively embedded into the developer workflow, credential sprawl is inevitable.”

Lewis agrees that the answer lies in the basics. “Another important note is that this highlights the need for getting the fundamentals right. Secrets shouldn’t live in source code. Credentials should be short-lived and rotated. Identity should follow least privilege. A compromised credential shouldn’t provide broad access across the enterprise. And organisations need automated controls in the development pipeline that can identify these problems before code is published or deployed.”

For Hogue-Spears, that means removing long-lived secrets from pipelines altogether. “Security leaders must move pipelines to managed identities or workload identity federation, which leave no secret to commit. A managed identity keeps whatever permissions an administrator grants it, so replace tenant-wide Microsoft Graph permissions with selected permissions scoped to the site or file the application needs. Treat any secret that reaches a public repository as compromised and revoke it in the identity provider before anyone cleans the Git history.”

Beyond leaked credentials

Not every finding involved a secret. At the Department for Education, the Get Help Buying for Schools service allowed anyone holding a valid request identifier to change request details – including the contact email – and submit the request without signing in; it was fixed on 10 July. In the department’s teacher application service, an account-linking code could overwrite an existing login association. Elsewhere, a long-lived administrator token was found embedded in public JavaScript on a Scottish Government open data portal, which has since been decommissioned.

Hogue-Spears highlighted a further DfE case as a lesson in authorisation testing. “In the Department for Education’s training-provider register, delete actions ran with no authorisation check, so a low-privileged staff account was able to soft-delete registered providers and other staff accounts. The same service’s user-editing policy did run, and it examined the record’s state, not the caller’s role, so a standard staff account was able to deactivate an administrator’s account. The department fixed both flaws in July. If your tests never sign in as an ordinary user and attempt an administrator’s action, a missing check and a wrong check both ship.”

Why closing the code won’t close the gap

The findings arrive as some in government question whether public bodies should keep repositories open in an era of AI-accelerated discovery. Nesbitt-Smith himself has warned that pulling code private without fixing the flaws could make risks harder to spot. The experts are unanimous on this point.

“Making a repository private hides the code, and a secret that leaked while the repository was public stays valid until it expires or someone revokes it,” said Hogue-Spears. “Leaders have to name an owner for every public repository. Since May, the UK government guidance has set a minimum before code goes public: a named owner and controls that stop developers from committing secrets.”

Maxwell is blunter. “Consequently, advising departments to pull their codebases private without remediating the underlying architectural flaws is incredibly dangerous. Security by obscurity has never stopped an advanced persistent threat. Closing the repositories simply blinds the independent research community that provides vital early warnings, while doing absolutely nothing to evict threat actors who already hold the compromised credentials.”

Lewis argues the real shift is in mindset. “Although there’s a knee jerk to blame AI for discovering weaknesses like this; in reality, a motivated attacker could have found these. AI doesn’t make design decision more dangerous; it simply changes the economics. In short, AI allows someone to search for existing mistakes, just faster, cheaper and at a scale that wasn’t practical in the past. And perhaps the most important lessons learned from this is that businesses need to operate under the assumption that if a weakness is discoverable, someone will eventually find it.”

Maxwell leaves the final word with a call for discipline rather than retreat. “We operate in a climate where the UK faces continuous, hostile cyber activity. There is a vast difference between falling victim to a highly sophisticated zero day exploit and simply handing adversaries your production logins. The government does not need to retreat into the shadows. It needs to mandate strict, automated security gates across the entire software supply chain and treat identity security with the rigorous operational discipline it demands.”

Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed. Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side. The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.” AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures. Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t. This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models. Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable. No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all. To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult. But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added: “Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.” Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history. These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems. This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.” The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive. These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers , 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately. What Muse owners can do Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe. With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected. If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device. From reporting threats to removing them. items.title: Grok AI App Builder Exposes Over 35,000 Apps, Leaking Confidential Business Data and Passwords
items.summary: Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords , and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them. Grok’s Build mode creates and publishes chat-generated apps under grok.me, while its parent company, SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), did not respond to Claroc but answered media questions on November 10, 2026. On November 8, 2026, Claroc researchers worked through a list of more than 43,500 grok.me addresses. They opened the first page of each app once, signed in to nothing, like any visitor in a private browser window. Of the 37,571 apps still online, 35,578 (94.7%) opened for Anyone. Only 1,993 asked for a sign-in. The list came from passive DNS, a service that records website name lookups and lets Anyone search them. Each Grok app gets its own address, so the name enters those records once someone opens the app. Grok AI App Builder Exposes Data The researchers say Grok’s four-random-word names are hard to guess, but nobody needs to guess them because the records list them. The same method exposed Meta’s Muse, as covered in our Meta Muse AI privacy flaw report . Most open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators. About one in ten held sensitive or internal data, and roughly 2% were serious enough to rate high or critical. SpaceXSI’s sales territory map (source: Claroc) Confirmed examples include an intensive care briefing with a patient’s labs and ventilator status, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 employees, and a fire department’s shift board with badge numbers. One contractor’s timesheet app held 18 staff accounts with plain-text passwords in code that every visitor’s browser downloads. SpaceXSI and X staff also left 24 apps open. They included a confidential onboarding plan, a sales map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals, one aimed at a U.S. federal agency. Another 30 identifiable organizations had internal data exposed. Of these, 26 have over 1,000 employees, and six are Fortune 500 companies. SpaceXSI took down its own 24 apps after the report, but not those of other users. Grok app links become publicly searchable through passive DNS records after their first use (source: Claroc) Claroc found that paid-account apps defaulted to public link access, allowing anyone to view and add records to apps without login protection. A team app with Google sign-in checked who the visitor was but not whether they belonged to the team. A stranger with a Google account could read, edit, and delete customer records. The researchers tested this only on their own apps. SpaceXSI says apps stay private until the creator shares them, and that publishing takes several steps. Claroc replies that every owner of the 35,578 open apps went through those same steps. Teams should find out which AI app builders their staff use, since tools like Lovable, Replit, and Grok need no IT approval. Check each app’s access settings, and test sign-in with an outside account. Look in the app’s script files for passwords and unpublish anything nobody owns. Unpublishing a grok.me app takes it offline within seconds. simplified from the code Grok wrote for us (source: Caroc ) This is not Grok’s first exposure problem. In 2025, more than 370,000 shared Grok chats appeared in Google search, which we covered in our report on Grok chats exposed in Google results . The comprehensive research is on the Claroc blog. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud
items.summary: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.
