items.title: Platform engineering needs to become more human…and less
items.summary: Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan. Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing. I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates. But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans. We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy. That is so Oct 2025 But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, every one changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me). Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million. What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite . They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. They name things for other humans, so production ends up running something called “Q4 launch page FINAL (Jen’s edits).” These aren’t really flaws. In most of the company, they’re called “initiative”. Or “creativity”. But you might also call it “chaos”. Of course, engineers are creative too. But what we’re about to see…what we’re already seeing…is an EXPLOSION in creativity entering the software development world. Because now creativity of all sorts, from all sorts of very non-robotic people, has been given direct access to the code. Musicians. Copywriters. Recruiters. The finance lead who has opinions about dashboards. These are people who were never going to learn a programming language, and now they don’t have to. They bring taste, empathy, and a feel for what customers want, which the old pipeline often filtered out long before anything reached production. They also bring their own idea of what “done” means and no idea how a typical internal developer platform operates. But these new humans and this explosion in creativity are here. And they’re not going away. So platform engineering has to find a way to harness all this creativity without it taking anything important offline or leaking company secrets all over the internet. Making room for the more-human builders Here’s what I think needs to happen for that to take place. The rules have to move out of people’s heads and into the platform. For as long as most of us have done this work, the guardrails lived inside the engineers…at least in large part. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one. Agents should do their work in preview environments that look like production but aren’t, and changes should reach production only through the same small, watched, self-reversing rollouts the humans use. Every action has to go into an audit trail that answers “which agent, launched by whom, to do what.” And there has to be a kill switch that someone can find in under a minute. Most importantly, the rules have to be written down, in a form a machine can read. The unwritten rules your platform used to depend on simply don’t exist for an agent. When it breaks one, the platform’s answer should be a clear, structured reason and the specific thing to change, so the agent fixes its request instead of hammering the same door 500 times. Here’s the good news. Once the rules are written down, agents become the most reliable builders you have. They don’t argue with the template, skip the checklist, or decide the standard doesn’t apply to them this one time. Before orchestration, running software at scale meant a person watching servers. Someone noticed a process had died and restarted it. Someone decided which machine had room. Someone approved every change. That worked with a dozen servers and fell apart at a thousand. Kubernetes didn’t fix it by hiring faster operators. It changed the contract between the operator and the work, and four parts of that contract map almost exactly onto the new builders. You declare, it reconciles. You don’t tell Kubernetes how to keep three replicas running. You say you want three, and a control loop works continuously to make it true. That’s what the new humans need. Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job.

If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane.

Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson.

Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand.

And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan.

Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing.

I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates.

But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. 

I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans.

We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy.

That is so Oct 2025

But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, everyone changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me).

Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million.

What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite. They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. They name things for other humans, so production ends up running something called “Q4 launch page FINAL (Jen’s edits).” These aren’t really flaws. In most of the company, they’re called “initiative”. Or “creativity”. But you might also call it “chaos”.

Of course, engineers are creative too. But what we’re about to see…what we’re already seeing…is an EXPLOSION in creativity entering the software development world. Because now creativity of all sorts, from all sorts of very non-robotic people, has been given direct access to the code. Musicians. Copywriters. Recruiters. The finance lead who has opinions about dashboards. These are people who were never going to learn a programming language, and now they don’t have to. They bring taste, empathy, and a feel for what customers want, which the old pipeline often filtered out long before anything reached production. They also bring their own idea of what “done” means and no idea how a typical internal developer platform operates.

But these new humans and this explosion in creativity are here. And they’re not going away. So platform engineering has to find a way to harness all this creativity without it taking anything important offline or leaking company secrets all over the internet.

Making room for the more-human builders

Here’s what I think needs to happen for that to take place.

The rules have to move out of people’s heads and into the platform.

For as long as most of us have done this work, the guardrails lived inside the engineers…at least in large part. Nobody had to tell a senior engineer not to expose a database to the internet, not to paste an API key into a chat window, or not to name a production table test. They’re doing what every smart, motivated person does with a new tool: click around until something lights up.

Secrets must get injected at runtime, not handed to a person, so there’s nothing to paste into Slack and nothing to save in a notes app for later. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Every deployment has to go out small, get watched, and roll itself back if the numbers turn bad.

When the platform does have to say no, it should say it the way a good colleague would. Not “Denied by policy 0042.” More like, “This would make your customer list public on the internet. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one.

Agents, the less-human builders

But wait a minute. We’ve had an explosion in human creativity entering the platform engineering chat, but we’ve also had a super explosion in agents…who are more robotic than any of (well, most of) the engineers I’ve ever worked with.

Here’s what I mean. An agent will read every line of your documentation, which already puts it ahead of most of us. It follows instructions exactly. When an agent hits a wall, it doesn’t stop to ask someone. It retries, and then tries another route, and then another, until it finds a path that’s open. Agents don’t learn the 2am lessons any more than the copywriter does. Most of them start every session fresh, with no memory of past outages and (just as important) none of the emotions that come with them.

So what do we do about these less-human engineers?

Every agent has to be treated as its own accountable actor, with limits set for machine speed rather than human speed.

That starts with identity. Every agent has to have its own identity, tied to the person who launched it, with permissions scoped to the task and an expiry that matches it. When the task ends, so does the access. Then it needs a speed limit: a cap on how many changes it can make, how many resources it can create, and how much it can spend in an hour, so a loop that would have done damage at machine speed hits a ceiling instead. Here’s the good news. Once the rules are written down, agents become the most reliable builders you have. They don’t argue with the template, skip the checklist, or decide the standard doesn’t apply to them this one time.

Taking a page from Kubernetes

I’m optimistic about our ability to build for these new platform users, and the reason is Kubernetes. We’ve solved this problem before. Just not for people.

It changed the contract between the operator and the work, and four parts of that contract map almost exactly onto the new builders.

You declare, it reconciles. You don’t tell Kubernetes how to keep three replicas running. You say you want three, and a control loop works continuously to make it true. That’s what the new humans need. The copywriter should be able to say “a landing page customers can reach, that can read the product catalog,” and the platform works out the identity, the network, the secrets, and the rollout. Agents get the same contract in its most literal form. A spec is exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at writing.

Every request goes through admission. Nothing gets into a cluster without passing the admission controllers, where policy can reject the request or fix it. A change from the designer, a change from an agent, and a change from Dan all go through the same door and get checked against the same written rules. There’s no VIP entrance for people who “know what they’re doing.” (Sorry, Dan.)

items.title: Claude Code AI Discovers Technique to Turn Dormant Model Neurons Into Hidden Malware Triggers
items.summary: Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons. Called Lazarus, the method plants a hidden backdoor in model weights, allowing an attacker’s trigger to make an AI agent produce commands that download and run malicious code. The model can still pass standard evaluations and behave normally during routine tasks. The findings expose a security gap for organizations giving AI agents access to terminals, files, and credentials. Unlike the malicious Claude Code extension reported separately, this technique does not depend on adding a malicious software loader. Instead, the dangerous behavior sits inside the model’s internal parameters, where ordinary application security checks may miss it. Claude Code AI Discovers Technique Microsoft researchers identified the Lazarus backdoor technique and detailed its malware-execution risk in research published on November 10, 2026. Microsoft Threat Intelligence stressed that it had not observed threat actors weaponizing the method. This is a demonstrated research attack, not a confirmed malware campaign, and Claude Code was the research assistant used to discover much of the technique. According to Microsoft’s original research explanation , principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos asked Claude Code, running Opus 4.5, to explore backdooring a model by hardwiring selected activations without training. The experiment developed into a broader study, with human researchers investigating the results and defenses. Lazarus targets neurons that rarely activate during normal operation. Researchers repurpose these quiet components as trigger detectors, using patterns already represented inside the pretrained model. A small set of examples helps separate inputs containing a chosen trigger from ordinary inputs, avoiding the cost of retraining the entire model. This differs from prompt injection attacks bypassing safeguards through hostile instructions: Lazarus changes the model itself before deployment. Its trigger can be an ordinary string appearing in the agent’s context, including information returned by a tool. The attacker must first obtain write access to the model checkpoint containing its weights. Each modified neuron can push one selected token into the residual stream, the internal pathway carrying information toward the model’s next output. Chaining several neurons lets the backdoor produce a complete command. Execution then depends on the surrounding agent software, available tools, and permissions; the model alone does not automatically control the host. In one example, a date change into 2027 activates the hidden behavior during an ordinary task. The agent emits a command that fetches and runs attacker-controlled code. Microsoft says the editing process needs only inference-level computing resources: hardware capable of running the model can also support this form of tampering. Detecting Hidden Model Changes and Limiting Damage The central defensive challenge is that normal answers do not establish model integrity. Earlier work on detecting backdoor attacks before deployment addresses the broader problem of models that behave correctly until triggered. Lazarus reinforces why behavioral evaluations should accompany, rather than replace, direct inspection of model weights. Microsoft recommends comparing every checkpoint against its declared original model before deployment and after updates. Legitimate modifications generally produce broader changes, while these implants can leave unusually large edits concentrated in a few weight vectors. Advanced AI agents can help flag suspicious structures, although Microsoft cautions that no audit guarantees safe behavior. Organizations should obtain models from original publishers, verify published file hashes, and keep approved checkpoints in access-controlled registries. Microsoft also distinguishes conventional model scanning from weight auditing: checks for embedded malware, unsafe operators, or exposed secrets do not replace examination of altered neural parameters. Containment remains essential because a triggered agent inherits its existing access. The same principle underlies Ghostjacking attacks against agents , where manipulated inputs can lead to dangerous tool use. Microsoft recommends least privilege, isolated code execution, restricted outbound connections, and human approval for consequential actions. Monitoring should also cover suspicious child processes and unexpected network activity. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator category Source disclosure SHA-256 or other hashes None published in the advisory Malicious domains or URLs None published in the advisory Attacker IP addresses None published in the advisory Weaponization status No threat actors observed using this technique Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities Allowing Hackers to Execute Malicious Code Through Cloned Repositories
items.summary: The Git project patched six vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw that allows malicious repositories to execute code during recursive cloning. The other five involve unsafe file writes and memory corruption in merges and patches. Git announced the fixes on November 10, 2026. The patches arrive in Git 2.56.1. They are also backported to 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. Users should move to 2.56.1 or the latest fix for their release line. Any app that ships its own copy of Git needs an update too. The most severe flaw is CVE-2026-111760, rated High with a CVSS score of 8.0. Git normally checks file paths before it writes them, and it blocks any path that would overwrite its own repository data. However, an integer truncation in the index code lets an extremely long path pass the check under one name and then get written under a shorter one. An attacker can use this to swap a submodule’s .git file for a symbolic link. The link points to a folder holding malicious settings or hooks. When Git later uses that folder, it runs the attacker’s code. Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities The advisory says this appears to need the –recurse-submodules option. The fix rejects overly long index paths before their length can be cut short. This is not the first time cloned repositories have caused trouble. Cyber Security News covered CVE-2025-48384 , which CISA confirmed as exploited, and a Lazarus Group campaign that used a similar symlink trick against developers. Those cases show how quickly attackers turn clone bugs into real attacks. CVE-2026-113408 affects cloning an empty repository over protocol v2. A malicious server can advertise a HEAD pointer with path-traversal pieces in its name. Git did not check it, so a later branch update could write outside the intended reference folder. Git now validates the target, along with other reference names it receives over protocol v2. CVE-2026-114467 is a stack memory bug. When Git removes GPG signatures from a message, it assumes there would be at most two. A crafted tag with more can overflow a fixed-size array. Merging that tag could corrupt memory or crash, and hosting services that merge on behalf of users may also be affected. CVE-2026-114469 involves binary patches. The Git project patched six vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw that allows malicious repositories to execute code during recursive cloning. The other five involve unsafe file writes and memory corruption in merges and patches. Git announced the fixes on November 10, 2026.

The patches arrive in Git 2.56.1. They are also backported to 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. Users should move to 2.56.1 or the latest fix for their release line. Any app that ships its own copy of Git needs an update too.

The most severe flaw is CVE-2026-111760, rated High with a CVSS score of 8.0. Git normally checks file paths before it writes them, and it blocks any path that would overwrite its own repository data.

However, an integer truncation in the index code lets an extremely long path pass the check under one name and then get written under a shorter one.

An attacker can use this to swap a submodule’s .git file for a symbolic link. The link points to a folder holding malicious settings or hooks. When Git later uses that folder, it runs the attacker’s code.

Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities

The advisory says this appears to need the –recurse-submodules option. The fix rejects overly long index paths before their length can be cut short.

This is not the first time cloned repositories have caused trouble. Cyber Security News covered CVE-2025-48384, which CISA confirmed as exploited, and a Lazarus Group campaign that used a similar symlink trick against developers. Those cases show how quickly attackers turn clone bugs into real attacks.

CVE-2026-113408 affects cloning an empty repository over protocol v2. A malicious server can advertise a HEAD pointer with path-traversal pieces in its name.

Git did not check it, so a later branch update could write outside the intended reference folder. Git now validates the target, along with other reference names it receives over protocol v2.

CVE-2026-114467 is a stack memory bug. When Git removes GPG signatures from a message, it assumes there would be at most two. A crafted tag with more can overflow a fixed-size array. items.title: Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities Allow Attackers to Bypass Security Feature
items.summary: Microsoft has disclosed two Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerabilities that could allow attackers with physical access to weaken device protections. Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97015 and CVE-2026-119832. Microsoft rates both as Important, with CVSS base scores of 6.8 and 5.9, respectively. The bugs have different causes and access requirements, so security teams should assess each separately. For CVE-2026-119832, Microsoft confirms that a successful attacker could bypass BitLocker Device Encryption on the system storage device and access encrypted data. The attack requires physical access and basic user privileges. It does not require another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a prompt. CVE-2026-97015 stems from a heap-based buffer overflow, classified as CWE-122 . This type of flaw occurs when software writes beyond the memory space reserved for a buffer. Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities Microsoft says an unauthorized attacker can use the weakness to bypass a security feature through a physical attack. No existing privileges or user interaction are required, and attack complexity is rated low. CVE-2026-119832 involves improper access control rather than a memory handling error. An attacker needs low privileges, but exploitation requires no user interaction. According to Microsoft’s advisory , the vulnerability was not publicly disclosed or known to be exploited at the time of release. Microsoft rates exploitation as less likely and credits researcher yhw. These disclosures follow earlier Windows BitLocker bypass vulnerabilities and the October 2026 BitLocker security updates . CVE-2026-119832 affects Windows 10 versions 1809, 21H2, and 22H2, several Windows 11 releases, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Supported processor platforms vary by release. CVE-2026-97015 has a broader affected product list that also includes older Windows Server branches. Administrators should check both records rather than rely on a single shared device list. Microsoft lists KB5131096 for affected Windows 10 21H2 and 22H2 systems, KB5131087 for Windows 11 23H2, and KB5132059 for Windows 11 26H1 under CVE-2026-119832. Server updates include KB5131085 for Server 2019 and KB5131090 for Server 2022. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday fixes Outlook flaw already under attack
items.summary: Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday fixes more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities , including an Outlook flaw that attackers are already exploiting to steal authentication information. The release also fixes 48 critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected machines, in some cases without user interaction. While Windows updates address many of this month’s vulnerabilities, readers should check for Office updates as well: the exploited Outlook flaw is patched through the affected Office products. To do this, follow these instructions: Open an Office application, such as Word. Go to File > Account . In Outlook, this may appear as Office Account . Under Product Information , select Update Options > Update Now . If necessary, select Enable Updates first. If the update controls are missing on a work device, contact your organization’s IT team; updates may be centrally managed. During the update, you may be prompted to save your work (check your open documents). Afterward, you should see something similar to this: Office updates installed How to apply Windows patches and check if you’re protected These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date: Click the Start button, then open Settings . Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left). Click Check for updates . Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options , you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update. You may find the update (Security Update KB5132061) already installed. Windows Update history If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update. After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date , you’re all set. Technical details As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details. We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194 , an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting . It has a CVSS score of 6.5 out of 10 and could expose authentication information that attackers could use to impersonate the user. From Microsoft’s description: “Product ui does not warn user of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.” To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must convince someone to open a specially crafted message file in an affected version of Outlook. This can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without its usual external-content warning, potentially exposing authentication information (the user’s NTLMv2 hash) that could be used to impersonate them. As this vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, updating Office as described earlier is a priority. One other vulnerability I want to highlight is CVE-2026-116928 (CVSS score 9.8 out of 10): “Out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.” An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use, which can lead to memory corruption or place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it. Microsoft describes an attack in which a malicious email attachment is processed automatically for indexing by Exchange Server. In that scenario, the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Processing it could be enough to let the attacker run code with the permissions of the affected service. Microsoft has not reported exploitation of this vulnerability. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

items.title: Multiple Windows Remote Desktop Flaws Allow Attackers to Execute Code Over Network
items.summary: Microsoft has released security updates for four Windows Remote Desktop Client vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code through network connections or local access. Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws involve memory handling errors and a race condition. Three have network attack paths, while the fourth requires an attacker with existing local access, an important difference when assessing exposure. The highest-scoring flaw, CVE-2026-119934, carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and an Important severity rating. Microsoft describes it as a double-free bug, meaning the client releases the same memory area more than once. This can damage memory handling and allow an attacker to run code when the affected client processes a response from a malicious server. An attacker would need to host that server and persuade a user to connect. No prior account access is required, but user interaction is necessary. This is not an attack where someone can simply send traffic to any Windows computer and gain control. The exposed component is the connecting Remote Desktop client, making the choice of remote server central to this attack path. CVE-2026-119858 involves a heap-based buffer overflow that allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. The flaw concerns data exceeding the space reserved for it in memory. Microsoft’s advisory says exploitation depends on specific conditions, such as protocol settings or configurations. Those requirements limit the likelihood of broad attacks, but do not remove the need to update affected clients. The race condition, CVE-2026-95964 , has a CVSS score of 7.5. It affects how client operations share a resource without proper synchronization. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, where operations occur in a particular order or timing. Microsoft lists user interaction as required and rates exploitation as unlikely, reflecting the added difficulty of reliably triggering this network code execution flaw. CVE ID Vulnerability Severity CVE-2026-119934 Double-free RCE High (8.8) CVE-2026-119858 Heap buffer and integer overflow RCE High (7.5) CVE-2026-119390 Heap buffer overflow enabling local code execution High (7.8) CVE-2026-95964 Race-condition RCE High (7.5) Remote Desktop Client Attack Conditions The fourth issue, CVE-2026-119390 , needs separate treatment despite its Remote Code Execution title. Microsoft’s technical description identifies a local heap-based buffer overflow requiring low privileges, with no additional user interaction. Its CVSS score is 7.8. Reporting it as an unauthenticated network attack would therefore misstate the access needed to exploit it. Client-side attacks are an established concern. Cyber Security News previously covered a Remote Desktop Client vulnerability involving a malicious server and a different underlying weakness. That earlier case provides useful context, but it is not evidence that the newly disclosed flaws share its attack method or have already been used against organizations. Social engineering also makes the connection step relevant. Previous rogue RDP phishing campaigns used emailed connection files to direct victims toward attacker-controlled servers. Those campaigns abused remote resource sharing rather than these new memory flaws. The connection is practical, not proof of a shared campaign: attackers already have methods for persuading users to open unwanted remote sessions. Affected Windows Systems Microsoft’s CVE-2026-119934 advisory lists affected Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server releases. Administrators should check each vulnerability’s product table rather than assume one update covers every installation. The CVE-2026-119390 table also includes Windows App Client for Windows Desktop, with version 2.0.1489.0 listed as the fixed build for that product. Security teams should deploy the matching updates and verify installation across employee devices and administrative systems that make Remote Desktop connections. Microsoft reported no exploitation at publication for CVE-2026-119934, CVE-2026-119390, and CVE-2026-95964. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
items.summary: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again. The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles. What CERT-In has confirmed The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges. Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends. CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it. How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account The advisories describe four stages: Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA. Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels. Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL. Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with. Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic. Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical The real story: AI took away the grace period Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage. What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list. That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't. Who's exposed Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request. What to do this week CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path: Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access. Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys. Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now. Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements. Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress. Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically. What we're watching The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure. Sources CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON" , Nov. 4, 2026 The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access , Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research) Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms , Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector , Nov. 5, 2026 Disclaimer: The data and content written in this blog is based on on open web information available. Analysts and researchers are advised to confirm once again from original sources.

  • Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

  • Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

  • Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

  • Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

  1. Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

  2. Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

  3. Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

  4. Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

  5. Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

  6. Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

Sources

CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON", Nov. 4, 2026

The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access, Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research)

Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms, Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector, Nov. 5, 2026

items.title: AI Agents Promise Convenience, But Are We Giving Them Too Much Control?
items.summary: AI agents are quickly becoming part of everyday life, moving beyond answering questions and generating content to carrying out tasks on users’ behalf. From booking holidays and managing diaries to making purchases and accessing personal accounts, the technology promises to make our lives easier than ever before. However, as AI agents become increasingly autonomous, questions are emerging about how much control people are willing to hand over and whether adequate safeguards are in place. Research commissioned by cybersecurity PR agency Eskenzi PR and conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK adults found that 84% would give AI agents only moderate or low control over their daily lives, or none at all . More than a third (34%) wouldn’t feel comfortable giving AI agents any control whatsoever, suggesting that while consumers recognise the potential benefits of AI, many remain hesitant about allowing it to act independently. Security concerns are holding back trust As AI agents gain greater access to sensitive information and personal accounts, the potential consequences of security failures become increasingly significant. Eskenzi’s research found that 36% of Brits are concerned about their personal data being hacked or stolen when using AI agents. Almost a third (31%) worry an AI agent could make a mistake, while 30% are concerned about it having access to too much personal information. Financial security is another major concern, with 28% worried that an AI agent could spend their money or make purchases they never intended to authorise. Perhaps most surprisingly, one in seven (14%) fear an AI agent could implicate them in something illegal, rising to 21% among 18 to 24-year-olds. These concerns highlight the security challenges associated with giving autonomous systems access to personal information and the ability to perform actions on behalf of users. Unlike traditional AI chatbots, which primarily generate responses to user prompts, AI agents may be connected to external applications and granted permissions to interact with accounts and services. This introduces potential risks around compromised credentials, excessive permissions and malicious instructions designed to manipulate an agent’s behaviour. For cybersecurity professionals, ensuring these systems operate within clearly defined boundaries will be essential to reducing the risks associated with wider adoption. People want assistance, not complete autonomy Despite concerns about security, the findings suggest that consumers are not rejecting AI entirely. Instead, they appear more comfortable using it as an assistant than allowing it to make important decisions independently. More than a quarter (27%) of respondents would allow an AI agent to prepare tasks for them but would want to approve every action. A further 23% would allow AI to handle routine tasks independently while requiring permission for more significant decisions. There are also clear generational differences. Almost half of over-55s (47%) would not give AI agents any control over their daily lives, compared with 21% of 18 to 24-year-olds. The findings suggest that organisations developing AI agents need to consider how much autonomy users are comfortable granting, rather than assuming greater independence will always be welcomed. Introducing meaningful human approval checkpoints, limiting agent permissions and ensuring users can review actions before they are completed could help organisations address some of these concerns. Who takes responsibility when AI goes wrong? Beyond security and privacy, the research raises important questions about accountability. When asked who should bear primary responsibility if an AI agent with access to their accounts was hacked, tricked or carried out an unauthorised action, 40% of respondents pointed to the company that developed the AI. A further 25% believed responsibility should sit with the company or service the agent was accessing, while only 18% thought the individual using the AI should be primarily responsible. While these findings reflect public expectations rather than legal liability, they demonstrate the importance of establishing clear accountability as autonomous systems become more widespread. The implications extend to businesses deploying AI agents in customer-facing and decision-making processes. When asked how they would react if a company they relied on used an AI agent to advise its board on important decisions, 37% wanted reassurance that a human would always have the final say. Meanwhile, 20% said they would consider switching provider, suggesting that concerns around AI oversight could also have reputational and commercial consequences. Building confidence through security and transparency AI agents have the potential to deliver significant improvements in convenience and productivity, but their growing autonomy creates new responsibilities for developers and organisations deploying the technology. Clear permission controls, secure authentication, monitoring, audit trails and human oversight can all play an important role in reducing risks and improving accountability. Equally important is ensuring that users understand what an AI agent can access, what actions it can perform and how they can intervene if something goes wrong. The research suggests that consumers are willing to embrace the benefits of AI, provided they can retain control over decisions that matter. As AI agents become more integrated into everyday life, the challenge for the cybersecurity industry will be ensuring that innovation is accompanied by the security, transparency and safeguards needed to earn public trust. The research was conducted by Censuswide among a nationally representative sample of 2,000 UK adults between 16 and 18 September 2026, on behalf of Eskenzi PR. Read the full Eskenzi PR research .

items.title: Finding it a day later isn’t protecting it
items.summary: In September, Delinea published new research on how AI behaves inside companies. Of the 2,254 IT and security leaders it surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent had accessed sensitive data beyond what its task needed in the past year. And 55% of organizations said it takes a full day or longer to catch an agent that steps outside its scope. The report also shows where the gap sits. 99.7% of organizations have a formal policy on what data AI tools and agents can access, but only 51% check access against that policy in real time. In a separate survey of 2,250 non-IT employees, 76% said they have bypassed the required approval to use AI, and 60% said they felt pressured to use AI on sensitive or confidential data when they weren’t sure it was allowed. Source: Delinea, 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap , Sept. 2026. Policies and approvals say what is allowed. They don’t change what is in the file when someone, or something, gets there anyway. PK Protect protects the file itself. What a data security platform does PK Protect finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i mainframes. It classifies what it finds under one classification policy, so the fix matches the data. Then it acts: encrypt it, mask it, or redact it. Part 2 compares this with DLP and DSPM. What changes about the day-long gap A late alert tells you what an agent reached. When PK Protect encrypts a file, the protection stays on the file after it moves. An agent that hasn’t been given access to the key can reach the file and still can’t read it. An agent working on a person’s behalf can open what that person can open, which is why controls on the agent still matter. This covers the file types PK Protect can protect. If someone keeps an unprotected original, that copy isn’t covered. On supported databases, warehouses, and cloud storage, sensitive values are masked instead, so there is no key. items.title: New GhostFrame Malware Lets Hackers Hijack VMware ESXi VMs and Steal Windows Credentials
items.summary: A new hacking toolkit called GhostFrame gives criminals a single control panel for taking over VMware ESXi servers and the virtual machines that run on them. Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group found the framework while tracking a group named TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware. The tool can also pull Windows passwords out of hosted machines without ever running a program inside them. The key point is where GhostFrame works. ESXi is a hypervisor, the layer that runs many virtual machines on one physical server. If a criminal controls that layer, they can reach every system on it. Security tools inside each virtual machine often cannot see what is happening below them. Insikt Group’s report says the framework does not exploit a bug to get in. The operator must already have root access to the ESXi host. GhostFrame Stays on the Server The framework has a web panel with two sections, “Sessions” and “Builder.” The builder creates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. Once it runs, it copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and edits the boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh so it starts again after every reboot. The script also turns off the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly setting, which normally blocks unsigned programs. It repeats this about every five seconds, so an administrator who turns the protections back on loses them again almost at once. The implant calls /sbin/auto-backup.sh to save its changes across restarts. It also renames itself vmhostd, which looks like VMware’s real vmware-hostd service, to hide in plain sight. The implant tries six network ports at the same time to reach its command server: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443. It keeps the first connection that works and drops the rest. If nothing connects within thirty seconds, it waits between five and twelve seconds and tries again. That pattern can show up as six nearly simultaneous connection requests from one ESXi host to one address, which gives defenders a useful clue to hunt for. After connecting, the implant loads code straight into memory and runs it, so nothing is written to disk. If it cannot get memory for that, it falls back to a plain /bin/sh reverse shell. GhostFrame lets an operator list virtual machines, change their power state, and create or delete snapshots. It can switch on VNC remote screen access and send the screen view through its own servers to the panel. It can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client, which is the management website for the hypervisor. A SOCKS5 proxy tool named gfsox lets operators send traffic through the host to reach internal systems that are hidden from the internet. The credential theft features matter most. A component called sdkmon changes the ESXi service setup and captures the usernames and passwords of later ESXi logins. GhostFrame also includes VMkatz, an open-source tool. It pulls secrets from VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, or a scan of every VM on a datastore. The data it can recover includes NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets, and NTDS.dit data. In short, a criminal can steal Windows passwords from the outside, with no malware installed in the guest. Link to Settra Ransomware and VPN Break-Ins Insikt Group watched TAG-218 servers go after VPN devices in the US and Europe from late August to October 2026. The targets were mostly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet products. Four of those victims later appeared on the Settra leak site. The same servers connected to two GhostFrame command servers and a MeshCentral server used to maintain access. On October 12, 2026, a Fortinet VPN device was seen contacting both GhostFrame and MeshCentral. Huntress had already tied MeshCentral to Settra. Its report shows the group installing MeshAgent for lasting access, using a vulnerable driver, clearing Windows logs, and blocking recovery. Our earlier coverage of the Settra ransomware and its MeshAgent tricks covers those steps in more detail. The timing matches the recent abuse of CVE-2026-0257, a flaw in Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that lets someone open a VPN session without valid credentials or MFA. Unit 42’s updated guidance says intruders moved from the VPN to the virtualization layer in one case. They turned off execInstalledOnly and used a custom tool to dump domain controller credentials straight from a virtual disk. That skips security software inside the guest. We reported on how hackers used this Palo Alto VPN flaw to steal credentials from VMware disks , and the GhostFrame findings fit the same pattern. Fixes for the Palo Alto flaw have been out since May 2026. Start by locking down who can reach ESXi. Allow management access only from trusted systems and look into any unexpected root logins or setting changes. Watch for edits to /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh, new files under /opt, and the repeated firewall and execInstalledOnly changes. Look at network logs for the burst of six connection attempts to one address. Patch VPN devices quickly and review the earlier reporting on ransomware groups targeting VMware ESXi for more hardening ideas. Insikt Group does not know if GhostFrame is limited to Settra or how it is shared. Still, it says it is highly likely that other money-driven criminals will use GhostFrame or similar ESXi tools. Treat your hypervisors as high-value systems and give them the same close watch you give domain controllers. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Critical Fortinet Flaws Expose FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer to Remote Code Execution Without Login
items.summary: Fortinet has disclosed critical security flaws affecting FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, and FortiOS, including weaknesses that could let attackers execute code without logging in. Published on November 10, 2026, the disclosures cover management APIs, device communication services, routing, and specific high availability setups. Attack requirements differ, making enabled features and network access central to assessing exposure. Critical Fortinet Flaws Patched The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-126170, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. Tracked as FG-IR-26-219 , it involves JSON injection in the JSON-RPC API used by FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer. When the JSON API is enabled, crafted requests could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code or commands. Systems using the API for automation need close review. Another critical flaw, CVE-2026-126261, affects FortiManager’s FGFM service. Rated 9.0 and tracked as FG-IR-26-275 , the authorization weakness allows attackers who can reach the FGFM port to send crafted packets and potentially execute code. The problem occurs before the registration password is verified, placing the service itself within the attack path. CVE-2026-126262, tracked as FG-IR-26-276 and rated 9.3, exposes FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager systems with FortiAnalyzer features enabled to SQL injection through OFTP. An attacker does not need to log in, and successful exploitation could lead to code execution. This makes access to the log transfer service an important part of exposure checks. The disclosures follow the October security releases previously covered in Cyber Security News’ Fortinet patch warning . Fortinet released updates before publishing the detailed advisories, giving customers time to upgrade. However, administrators should not assume that installing one October build resolves every November finding, because fixes vary by vulnerability and software branch. Fortinet’s FGFM advisory lists FortiManager 8.0.0, 7.6.0 through 7.6.7, 7.4.0 through 7.4.5, and 7.2.0 through 7.2.8 as affected by CVE-2026-126261. Fixed releases are 8.0.1, 7.6.8, 7.4.6, and 7.2.9, respectively. Fortinet marks this issue as not known to have been exploited when published. CVE-2026-126260, tracked as FG-IR-26-274, adds a separate OFTP risk. Rated 9.0, this pre-authentication server-side request forgery flaw affects FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager with FortiAnalyzer features enabled. It should not be confused with confirmed remote code execution. Its impact involves causing the server to make requests, while the SQL injection issue provides a different attack path. These weaknesses also show why protecting the browser login page is not enough. FGFM uses TCP port 541, while OFTP uses TCP port 514. Fortinet has disclosed critical security flaws affecting FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, and FortiOS, including weaknesses that could let attackers execute code without logging in.

Published on November 10, 2026, the disclosures cover management APIs, device communication services, routing, and specific high availability setups. Attack requirements differ, making enabled features and network access central to assessing exposure.

Critical Fortinet Flaws Patched

The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-126170, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. Tracked as FG-IR-26-219, it involves JSON injection in the JSON-RPC API used by FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer. When the JSON API is enabled, crafted requests could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code or commands. Systems using the API for automation need close review.

Another critical flaw, CVE-2026-126261, affects FortiManager’s FGFM service. Rated 9.0 and tracked as FG-IR-26-275, the authorization weakness allows attackers who can reach the FGFM port to send crafted packets and potentially execute code. The problem occurs before the registration password is verified, placing the service itself within the attack path.

CVE-2026-126262, tracked as FG-IR-26-276 and rated 9.3, exposes FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager systems with FortiAnalyzer features enabled to SQL injection through OFTP. An attacker does not need to log in, and successful exploitation could lead to code execution. This makes access to the log transfer service an important part of exposure checks.

The disclosures follow the October security releases previously covered in Cyber Security News’ Fortinet patch warning. Fortinet released updates before publishing the detailed advisories, giving customers time to upgrade. However, administrators should not assume that installing one October build resolves every November finding, because fixes vary by vulnerability and software branch.

Fortinet’s FGFM advisory lists FortiManager 8.0.0, 7.6.0 through 7.6.7, 7.4.0 through 7.4.5, and 7.2.0 through 7.2.8 as affected by CVE-2026-126261. Fixed releases are 8.0.1, 7.6.8, 7.4.6, and 7.2.9, respectively. Fortinet marks this issue as not known to have been exploited when published.

CVE-2026-126260, tracked as FG-IR-26-274, adds a separate OFTP risk. Rated 9.0, this pre-authentication server-side request forgery flaw affects FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager with FortiAnalyzer features enabled. It should not be confused with confirmed remote code execution. Its impact involves causing the server to make requests, while the SQL injection issue provides a different attack path.

These weaknesses also show why protecting the browser login page is not enough. FGFM uses TCP port 541, while OFTP uses TCP port 514. Administrative login restrictions do not directly protect those services. Earlier FortiManager compromise reporting showed how access to a central management appliance could expose sensitive information linked to hundreds of managed firewalls.

Routing and Access Controls Also Affected

The broader release includes CVE-2026-126254, a 9.6-rated numeric truncation flaw in FortiOS BGP handling that requires traffic from a configured iBGP neighbor. CVE-2026-126253, rated 9.3, concerns an OSPF authentication bypass that could permit forged routing advertisements. These are routing risks, not interchangeable examples of management server code execution.

CVE-2026-126229, rated 9.1, could allow an authenticated administrator to access other virtual domains, or VDOMs, outside their permitted scope. Separately, CVE-2026-126259 carries a 9.0 rating and allows command execution with super-admin privileges in specific FortiOS setups involving FGSP with standalone configuration synchronization, or affected autoscale configurations. Neither issue should be described as affecting every deployment equally.

Fortinet’s security release guidance urges customers to prioritize exposed systems, back up configurations, and monitor unauthorized changes. For CVE-2026-126170, the 8.0 branch requires particular attention because 8.0.3 was listed as forthcoming. Disabling unused JSON API access with set rpc-permit none reduces exposure while administrators verify the latest advisory and plan the appropriate update.

items.title: Microsoft Confirms Hackers Are Exploiting Outlook 0-Day to Steal Windows Authentication Hashes
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that hackers are exploiting an Outlook zero-day that can expose Windows authentication information when a user opens a malicious file. Tracked as CVE-2026-124194, the spoofing vulnerability was patched on November 10, 2026. Microsoft marks it “Exploitation Detected” and says it was not publicly disclosed before the update. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 6.5 and a Moderate severity rating. However, confirmed attacks make it a patching priority. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index states that “Exploitation Detected” means the company knows of actual exploitation, not just that attackers could develop a working exploit. Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability An attacker does not need an account or prior access to the target’s system. Instead, they send a specially crafted message file and convince the recipient to open it in an affected Outlook version. Successful exploitation requires both user interaction and network connectivity. Opening the file can cause Outlook to connect to a network location controlled by the attacker without showing its usual external-content warning. Microsoft classifies the underlying weakness as CWE-356, where a product’s interface fails to warn users about unsafe actions. The missing warning removes an important chance to stop the connection. Microsoft explicitly states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Simply previewing a message does not meet the documented exploitation requirements. That separates this flaw from earlier Outlook attacks covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Russian hackers exploiting Outlook , which involved a different vulnerability requiring no user action. According to Microsoft’s advisory , successful exploitation discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash, potentially allowing an attacker to authenticate as that user. This is authentication-data theft, not evidence that the flaw directly runs malicious code. Microsoft rates confidentiality impact as High, with no direct integrity or availability impact. NTLM-related leaks can support follow-on attacks, depending on the receiving service’s protections. Microsoft’s earlier Outlook investigation documented authentication relay and offline password cracking as possible uses of captured Net-NTLMv2 data. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of compromised Ubiquiti routers shows how attackers previously used external infrastructure for credential theft. Those historical details do not establish attribution for this new campaign. Affected Versions Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024, across 32-bit and 64-bit editions. Microsoft lists fixed builds 16.0.14334.21048 for LTSC 2021 and 16.0.17932.21140 for LTSC 2024. Administrators should deploy the applicable Office security updates promptly. As added protection, Microsoft recommends blocking unnecessary outbound SMB traffic on TCP port 445 to the internet. This limits external SMB exposure but does not replace installing the Outlook fix. Affected product Architecture Fixed build / security update Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise 32-bit Install the applicable November 2026 security update for the deployed update channel. Microsoft does not list a single fixed build in the advisory. Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise 64-bit Install the applicable November 2026 security update for the deployed update channel. Microsoft does not list a single fixed build in the advisory.
